Project description:
MetaGuard is a schema impact analysis engine that integrates directly into 
GitHub CI/CD pipelines. When a developer opens a pull request containing a 
SQL migration, MetaGuard automatically parses the schema changes, traverses 
the downstream data lineage graph via OpenMetadata, scores the blast radius 
by severity and confidence, and posts a concise impact report as a PR comment 
before anything is merged. It catches breaking changes like dropped columns 
or incompatible type alterations that would silently break downstream tables, 
dashboards, and pipelines. The engine supports column-level lineage traversal, 
multi-change PR stress testing, calibrated severity tuning (CRITICAL to LOW), 
and an optional LLM summarizer (OpenAI / Groq) for plain-English explanations. 
It falls back gracefully to fixture-based mock mode when the live metadata 
instance is unreachable, ensuring CI never fails silently.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
i have used openmeta in two ways: 

1. MCP Server (primary transport): MetaGuard queries the OpenMetadata MCP 
endpoint at /mcp to fetch downstream lineage graphs for any affected entity. 
Given a fully qualified table name (e.g. acme_nexus_analytics.ANALYTICS.MARTS.fact_orders), 
the MCP server returns the full lineage tree — all downstream tables, views, 
dashboards, and pipelines — which MetaGuard traverses up to a configurable 
depth (default: 5 hops).

2. REST API (fallback transport): When MCP is unavailable, MetaGuard falls 
back to OpenMetadata's REST API to fetch the same lineage and asset metadata 
directly.

We ran MetaGuard against the live OpenMetadata sandbox at 
sandbox.open-metadata.org throughout development and testing. The sandbox 
provided real lineage graphs with sample assets (fact_orders ->customer_metrics ->  executive_sales_summary) which we used to validate our severity scoring, 
confidence penalization for deep hops, and column-level lineage detection. 
OpenMetadata's governance tags and asset ownership metadata are also read 
and surfaced in the impact report's suggested follow-up section.
How was your hackathon experience?:
genuinely one of the most focused and well-structured hackathons I have 
participated in. The problem space metadata, lineage, and data quality 
is something that doesn't get enough tooling attention despite being a daily 
pain point for data and platform engineering teams. Having OpenMetadata as 
the foundation was the right call; the MCP server and REST API are well 
documented and the sandbox made it possible to build and test against real 
lineage data without any infrastructure overhead.

Project description:
FluxGuardian is an AI-powered GitHub bot that prevents breaking database schema changes from reaching production.

THE PROBLEM: Every data team has lost critical time to silent schema breakage. Meta renamed a column in their Ads API, and marketing dashboards read zero for weeks. Uber lost $45M after a schema change miscalculated driver commissions for months. Equifax's 147M-record breach was partly because nobody tracked what PII lived where. OpenMetadata already knows the lineage—nobody consults it before merging.

OUR SOLUTION: FluxGuardian watches every PR with SQL migrations, parses the schema change, queries OpenMetadata's column-level lineage graph, and uses Claude AI to post a rich markdown comment explaining exactly what breaks, who to notify, PII warnings, governance gaps, and a safe migration plan—all in 10 seconds, before merge.

MULTI-SURFACE INTELLIGENCE: Not just a GitHub bot. Includes Slack slash command, Claude Desktop MCP server, and a polished React dashboard with live lineage visualization. Engineers get the same intelligence wherever they work.

IMPACT: Shifts breaking-change discovery from "production incident" to "pre-merge comment." Transforms OpenMetadata's rich metadata into active, shift-left governance. 181 tests passing. Production patterns throughout. Open-source MIT licensed.

"OpenMetadata has the metadata. FluxGuardian makes it active."
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
FluxGuardian uses OpenMetadata as its intelligence backbone—not just one API, but the full platform:

1. LINEAGE API (/api/v1/lineage/{entity}/name/{fqn}): We walk downstream edges at column-level to find every affected dashboard, pipeline, and ML model when a column is renamed, dropped, or altered. This is the core blast radius computation.

2. CLASSIFICATIONS: We check PII/PHI/Financial tags on columns to raise compliance warnings (GDPR implications, governance approval requirements) in the auto-generated PR comments.

3. OWNERSHIP: We resolve owner email → Slack handle for @mentions in PR comments, ensuring notifications reach the right engineers. Unassigned owners are flagged as governance gaps.

4. SEARCH API (/api/v1/search/query): For discovering assets that match SQL identifiers extracted from diff parsing.

5. GOVERNANCE POLICIES: We flag when sensitive PII columns are modified and approval requirements aren't documented.

6. GLOSSARIES: Extract business context for affected terms to enrich PR comments with domain knowledge.

Our MCP server exposes these as 6 Claude-callable tools (search_assets, get_column_lineage, get_blast_radius, find_owner, list_pii_columns, get_table_schema), making OpenMetadata accessible via natural language in Claude Desktop.

We seeded a realistic "FoodieExpress" demo with 5 tables, 4 dashboards, 2 ML models, 2 pipelines, PII classifications, and full column-level lineage to demonstrate these integrations work end-to-end.

Without OpenMetadata, FluxGuardian is impossible. We've built the "active governance" layer directly on top of OM's rich metadata foundation, turning passive documentation into shift-left automation that prevents production incidents.

Absolutely loved it! Building FluxGuardian pushed us to really explore OpenMetadata's capabilities deeply. The lineage API, classifications, and ownership metadata are incredibly well-designed and made blast radius analysis tractable. The MCP protocol integration with Claude Desktop was elegant and opened our eyes to the future of AI-powered data tools.

Key learnings:

Project description: Automated repair suggestions for failed OpenMetadata Data Quality checks
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
I've used OpenMetadata as a read-only source of truth for data quality failures. 
It connects to OpenMetadata's REST API to fetch failed Data Quality test cases, then pulls supporting context — table sample data, table/column profiler stats, and test result details — to analyze why a test failed. 
Based on the test definition type (e.g., null checks, uniqueness, regex matches), the app selects a fix strategy and generates SQL suggestions with confidence scores. 
The full OM 1.6.2 stack runs locally via Docker Compose, and the app never writes anything back to OpenMetadata — it only reads from it to power its analysis and fix-suggestion pipeline.
How was your hackathon experience?:
The hackathon was a deep dive into OpenMetadata's internals — working directly with its REST API meant a lot of trial and error, especially around quirks like the API returning 500s instead of 404s for missing resources and test definition types not always being included in responses. 
Setting up the full OM stack locally with Docker Compose had its own challenges getting all the services (MySQL, Elasticsearch, Airflow, the OM server) to play nicely together. 
On the learning side, I got a solid understanding of how OM models data quality — test cases, entity links, FQNs, table/column profiling — and how to build a meaningful layer on top of it. 
It was a very good exercise in shipping end-to-end under time pressure, from infrastructure to backend logic to a working UI.

Project description:
MetaGuard AI is an AI-powered data governance copilot built on OpenMetadata. It solves the universal problem of metadata debt; most data teams have hundreds of tables with missing descriptions, untagged PII columns, and no governance oversight.
MetaGuard has three core features:

PII Auto-Scanner: An AI agent (Gemini 2.5 Flash) scans table columns and classifies each as PII Sensitive, PII Non-Sensitive, or Not PII based on column names, data types, and descriptions. Users can approve classifications with one click, and the PII tag is written directly back to OpenMetadata via the PATCH API.
Governance Health Dashboard: A real-time governance score (0–100) computed from description coverage, column tag coverage, and table-level tag coverage pulled from OpenMetadata's Tables API. Includes animated score ring, progress bars, and metric breakdowns.
Natural Language Metadata Chat: Users ask metadata questions in plain English, like "Which tables have PII columns?" or "What happens if I drop the customers table?" The AI agent determines the right OpenMetadata API to query (tables, lineage, search), fetches the data, and returns a structured markdown-formatted answer.

Tech stack: Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and the OpenMetadata 1.12 REST API.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
MetaGuard AI integrates deeply with OpenMetadata across 10+ REST API endpoints:

GET /api/v1/tables — Lists all tables with columns and tags for the dashboard metrics and PII scanner table list
GET /api/v1/tables/name/{fqn} — Fetches detailed column-level metadata (name, dataType, description, existing tags) for AI-powered PII classification
PATCH /api/v1/tables/{id} — Writes PII classification tags (PII.Sensitive, PII.NonSensitive) back to specific columns after user approval, using JSON Patch format
PATCH /api/v1/tables/name/{fqn} — Adds descriptions to tables programmatically
GET /api/v1/lineage/table/name/{fqn} — Retrieves upstream and downstream lineage data for the chat agent to answer impact analysis questions
GET /api/v1/search/query — Full-text search across the table search index, used by the chat agent for keyword-based table discovery
PUT /api/v1/services/databaseServices — Programmatic database service creation
PUT /api/v1/databases — Database entity creation via API
PUT /api/v1/databaseSchemas — Schema entity creation via API
PUT /api/v1/tables — Table and column creation with full schema definitions, including data types and descriptions

The governance dashboard computes a health score by aggregating metadata completeness metrics directly from OpenMetadata's table data: description coverage, column tag coverage, and table-level tag coverage. The PII scanner creates a feedback loop: scan columns with AI → approve tags → tags are written to OpenMetadata → governance score improves. The chat agent uses OpenMetadata as its knowledge base, routing natural language questions to the appropriate API endpoint and synthesising the response.

Project description:
I built VAANI , it is  an intelligent observability and governance layer for OpenMetadata to act as a smart bridge for OpenMetadata. It’s an observability tool that catches technical webhook signals and uses Gemini 3 Flash to turn those messy JSON updates into clear governance insights and instant alerts that actually make sense to humans.

How it actually works:

The Catch: My backend picks up the technical signal from an OpenMetadata webhook.

The Brains: Instead of just logging it, I pass that data to Gemini 3 Flash. The AI looks at what changed and explains the actual risk in plain English.

The Record: Every event gets saved in a MongoDB Atlas cluster. This creates a "Governance Audit Trail," so you can basically travel through time to see how an asset has evolved.

The Loop: Finally, it finds the owner’s info from the metadata and sends them a clean, AI-summarized email via Nodemailer so they can take action immediately
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
my project is built directly on top of OpenMetadata’s Event-Driven Architecture. Instead of building a static dashboard that requires manual data entry, I used OpenMetadata as the "source of truth" for every data asset.

The Webhook Integration:
I set up a dedicated Node.js listener that connects to OpenMetadata via Webhooks. Every time a ChangeEvent occurs—like a schema being modified, a new tag being added, or an ownership change—OpenMetadata "pushes" a JSON payload to my backend. This is where the magic happens. VAANI doesn't just store this JSON; it parses the "entity" and "change" details to understand exactly what broke or moved.

Metadata Context for AI:
I didn't just use AI for the sake of it. I take the specific technical metadata fetched from OpenMetadata (like column types and descriptions) and feed it into Gemini 3 Flash. This allows the AI to provide a "Governance Summary" that is actually grounded in real metadata facts. It identifies the Data Owner directly from the OpenMetadata registry so that the final alert is sent to the right person.

Persistent Audit Trail:
Finally, I used the metadata signals to build a Governance Timeline in MongoDB. Since OpenMetadata tracks the evolution of an asset, I captured those state changes to create a persistent history. This means a user can look at the VAANI dashboard and see the entire lifecycle of an OpenMetadata entity—from its creation to its most recent schema drift—all summarized in plain English.

Project description: kubectl-style CLI for OpenMetadata - explore lineage, manage tags, query data quality, and govern your metadata catalog directly from the terminal.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
REST API as the backbone — every command calls OpenMetadata's /api/v1/ endpoints directly via HTTP, using Bearer JWT authentication

Search API (/api/v1/search/query) — powers omctl get and omctl search, querying OpenMetadata's Elasticsearch-backed search indexes (table_search_index, dashboard_search_index, etc.) with filters for service name and tag FQN

Entity API (/api/v1/tables/name/{fqn}, /api/v1/dashboards/name/{fqn}, etc.) — powers omctl describe, fetching full entity detail including columns, tags, owners, usage summary, and constraints by fully-qualified name

Lineage API (/api/v1/lineage/{entityType}/name/{fqn}) — powers omctl lineage show and omctl lineage impact, retrieving the full upstream/downstream graph with configurable depth

Data Quality API (/api/v1/dataQuality/testSuites, /api/v1/dataQuality/testCases) — powers omctl quality, fetching test suites, individual test cases, and their pass/fail result summaries

Classification & Tag API (/api/v1/classifications, /api/v1/tags) — powers omctl tag classifications, listing all tag categories defined in OpenMetadata

JSON Patch for tag mutations (PATCH /api/v1/tables/{id}) — powers omctl tag add and omctl tag remove, applying RFC 6902 JSON Patch operations to modify the tags array on any entity without overwriting other fields

User Login API (/api/v1/users/login) — powers omctl config login, exchanging email/password for a JWT access token that is then stored locally for all subsequent requests

Services API (/api/v1/services/databaseServices, etc.) — powers omctl get services, listing all registered data source connections across database, dashboard, pipeline, messaging, and storage service types

Project description:
A CLI tool that extends OpenMetadata's data profiler with 6 advanced statistical metrics — going beyond the standard basic stats. Followed the idea proposed over #26662

It works in three steps:

1. Configure — provide the OM and DB credentials, along with tables/schema for which you want to perform profiling. 

Supports schema-level wildcards (schema.*) to profile all tables in one go. JDBC connection details can be auto-discovered from OM's database service config, or provided explicitly.

Supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, MSSQL, Redshift, and Snowflake. 

2. Run — the tool connects to your database via JDBC, samples data using dialect-aware SQL, and computes per-column metrics based on column type.

3. Report — pushes all computed values back to OM as registered custom metrics (shows up natively in the Profiler tab with timeseries graphs), and generates a local HTML dashboard with per-table health scores, color-coded ratings, and metric interpretations.

Built with Java 21, JDBC, and OkHttp. Includes demo data (clean vs dirty table) to demonstrate how each metric catches specific data quality problems.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
Integrated deeply with OM's API across the tool:

- Authenticates via the login endpoint to get a JWT
- Fetches table schemas and column metadata using the tables API
- Auto-discovers JDBC connection details from OM's database service config — so users just provide an FQN and DB credentials, no need to manually look up hostnames and ports
- Expands schema wildcards (schema.*) using the paginated listTables endpoint
- Registers custom metric definitions via the customMetric API — this is required before values show up in the OM UI
- Pushes computed profiles using the tableProfile API, which appends to OM's timeseries — so repeated runs build line charts in the Profiler tab
- Pulls 90 days of profile history to compute seasonality (detects repeating row-count patterns across profiler runs)

In short, the tool treats OM as both the source & destination.

Reads from it, computes heavily, writes back to it silently.

The system runs in three independent modes simultaneously: a fully autonomous background worker that runs on a configurable schedule, an interactive Streamlit dashboard for data engineers who want visibility and control, and an MCP server that lets AI clients converse with your data platform naturally. All three share the same OpenMetadata tooling layer and the same Cerebras-powered intelligence.
This is what data platform governance looks like when you give it an autonomous agent brain

Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
OpenMetadata is the entire data backbone of DataSentinel.
Every piece of intelligence DataSentinel produces comes from the OpenMetadata REST API. Here's specifically how:
As the data source for monitoring — monitor.py queries OpenMetadata every cycle to pull the full table inventory, identify unowned tables, identify undocumented tables, fetch all ingestion pipeline statuses, and retrieve data quality test results. This is what feeds the health score calculation.
As the remediation target — when DataSentinel detects a failed ingestion pipeline, it calls the OpenMetadata API to retrigger that pipeline automatically via tools.trigger_pipeline(). OpenMetadata is not just read — it's written back to.
As the knowledge base for the AI agent — the conversational agent in agent.py uses OpenMetadata as its live context. When you ask "which tables have no owners?" the Cerebras LLM doesn't guess — it calls tools.get_unowned_tables() which hits the OpenMetadata API and returns real data. Same for lineage, quality failures, and pipeline status.
As the source for MCP tools — all 7 tools exposed by the MCP server are essentially OpenMetadata API calls wrapped with AI. When Claude Desktop or any MCP client connects to DataSentinel, it's getting live OpenMetadata data back.
The specific OpenMetadata entities used:

Tables and their ownership + description metadata
Ingestion pipelines and their run status
Data quality test results and failures
Table lineage graphs (upstream and downstream)

In short — OpenMetadata is not a supporting tool in this project. It is the platform DataSentinel exists to protect.
How was your hackathon experience?:

The hardest part wasn't the code — it was designing the policy layer. Deciding what an autonomous agent should fix on its own versus what it should escalate to a human is a genuinely hard problem and getting that right felt like the most important architectural decision in the entire project.


What surprised me most was how much the pieces fit together. OpenMetadata as the data backbone, Cerebras for speed, LangGraph for orchestration, MCP as the universal interface — each one solving a specific problem cleanly. By the end DataSentinel wasn't just a hackathon project, it was a system I'd actually want running on a real data platform.


This hackathon didn't just teach me new tools. It taught me how to think about autonomous systems — what it means to build something that acts safely, explains itself, and knows its own limits.

Project description:

Every dataset AfriGen generates is automatically registered in OpenMetadata with full column schema, lineage tracking from the Gemini AI pipeline to the output table, and a fidelity score that tells you exactly how trustworthy your data is. Not just data generation, but a full data infrastructure.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
AfriGen integrates OpenMetadata as its core governance layer through the REST API. Every dataset generated by the platform is automatically:

1. Registered as a Table Entity under a custom `afrigen-synthetic` Database Service with full column schema
2. Tagged with governance metadata including domain, country, fidelity score, and generation prompt
3. Tracked with lineage - OpenMetadata records that every table was produced by the `Gemini AI Generator` pipeline, grounded in WHO and World Bank statistics
4. Stored in a discoverable catalog that the AfriGen UI pulls from live via the OpenMetadata API

The integration covers REST API, database services, table entities, lineage edges, pipeline services, governance tags, and schema registration, built entirely from the Next.js backend using the OpenMetadata v1 API.
How was your hackathon experience?:
This hackathon broke me. Then it built me back.

I'm building from Lagos, Nigeria. And one of the first things this project demanded was getting OpenMetadata running locally, which meant pulling over 6GB of Docker images. On mobile data.
I watched my data disappear in real time. Gigabyte after gigabyte. Images pulling, failing, retrying, failing again - on a connection that was never designed for this. By the time I'd burned through 10GB, the containers still wouldn't start.
I almost quit. More than once.
But the idea wouldn't let me go. African ML engineers deserve proper data infrastructure. That belief was the only thing holding me to my chair at 2am, watching Docker logs scroll through another failure.
Then came actually registering the dataset, and that was its own war. 403 errors. Wrong API formats. Sandbox permission issues. Custom field validation breaking in ways I didn't understand yet. Every time I thought I'd fixed something, the next wall appeared. It was my first time working with OpenMetadata and Docker together, and it showed.
But I stayed in it.
And then it worked.
I opened the lineage tab. Saw the flow. Gemini AI Generator → table. Clean. Connected. Real.
I just stared at it for a second.
That one moment made every dropped connection, every 403, every hour of burned data worth it.
AfriGen isn't just a project. It's proof that African developers can build world-class data infrastructure from Lagos, on mobile data, against every odd stacked against us.
We just need the chance to show it.

Project description:
India's DPDP Act 2023 came into effect with penalties up to ₹250 crore per violation — and most fintech companies have no idea which of their database columns contain Aadhaar numbers, PAN cards, or biometric data. They're running on manual spreadsheets, quarterly audits, and hope. I built Agies AI to fix that.  Agies AI is a real-time PII governance engine that plugs directly into OpenMetadata. It automatically scans every table and column in your data catalog using a 3-layer AI pipeline — first catching obvious columns by name, then digging deeper with regulatory regex patterns, and finally using a FAISS semantic search engine (running ONNX embeddings locally, offline, in under 2ms per column) to catch obfuscated and aliased columns that a simple keyword scanner would completely miss. A column named col_x storing Aadhaar numbers? It catches that.Beyond scanning, it enforces governance in real-time. Every query a data analyst types — "show me all Aadhaar numbers from the users table" — gets run through an 11-ring deterministic pipeline that scores it, maps it to specific regulation sections (DPDP §4, GDPR Art. 9, HIPAA §164.514), and returns a BLOCK or ALLOW decision with a causal explanation in under 2 seconds. The decision is never a guess — it's grounded in actual regulation text, with penalty  exposure stated in rupees and euros.

The compliance report it generates isn't a developer dashboard — it's a board-ready document: overall compliance score, total penalty exposure in crore and millions, per-regulation breakdown, and a prioritized remediation roadmap. The kind of document a DPO would actually  hand to their CISO.
 On top of all this, I exposed 6 governance tools via the Model Context Protocol — so any AI agent (Claude, GPT,Gemini) can govern a data catalog through natural language, without a human in the loop.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
OpenMetadata isn't a background dependency in this project — it's the backbone. Every output Agies AI produces lives inside OpenMetadata's own data model, not in a parallel system.

  Here's specifically how I used it:

  1. Authentication & Catalog Discovery
  om_client.py authenticates against OM's /api/v1/users/login to get a JWT token, then fetches all tables with full column metadata via /api/v1/tables?fields=columns,tags. That column list is the direct input to the PII scanner — realschema definitions, not guesses.

  2. Custom Classification Taxonomy
  Before tagging, I programmatically create a Ageis  classification inside OpenMetadata with tags like DPDP_CRITICAL, GDPR_SPECIAL_CATEGORY, HIPAA_PHI, and PCI_DSS_RESTRICTED — each with the exact regulation citation as its description. This isn't OM's generic PII tag. Each tag carries regulatory identity, not just "this column has PII."

  3. Automated Tag Writeback
  After scanning, om_tagger.py writes the detected tags back to each column via PATCH /api/v1/tables/{id}. OpenMetadata becomes the single source of truth — a DPO checking the catalog in OM sees Agies AI tags directly, not in a separate tool. Every downstream OM feature — lineage, data quality, search — automatically inherits the compliance context.

  4. Compliance Aggregation
  om_compliance.py aggregates scan results into regulation-level summaries: how many CRITICAL columns exist, which regulations are triggered, total penalty exposure in ₹ crore and € millions. The compliance report is built on top of what was written back to OM — not computed independently.

  5. MCP Integration
  All 6 MCP tools — scan_table, scan_catalog, get_compliance_report, get_column_analysis, check_query_governance, get_audit_history — wrap the OM integration layer. An AI agent calling scan_catalog triggers real OM API calls, real PII detection, and real tag writeback, all through a single tool invocation.

  The design principle throughout: OpenMetadata should evolve from a passive catalog into an active governance layer —aware of risk, automatically tagged, and audit-ready — without a human ever touching a column tag manually.
How was your hackathon experience?:
● Honestly, this was one of the more intense weeks I've had building something.

  The idea came from a real frustration — I was reading about DPDP Act 2023 going into effect and realized that the  tools available to actually implement it at the data catalog level were either enterprise-priced, GDPR-only, or completely manual. OpenMetadata had all the right primitives — classifications, tag taxonomy, column-level metadata —but no automated governance layer sitting on top of it. That gap felt worth filling.

  The build started with design decisions that turned out to matter a lot:
  - A single LLM call for governance decisions didn't work — hallucinated regulation citations, inconsistent scores, 2–3 second latency per query. That's how the 11-ring deterministic pipeline came to be, where the LLM only enriches at Ring 9 and never makes the actual decision.
 - Getting the 3-layer scanner to catch obfuscated columns — not just aadhaar_number but col_x and hash_field_1 — took more iteration than expected. FAISS inference on CPU ended up being the right call: under 2ms per column, zero external API calls, works fully offline.

  Deployment had its own drama:
  - Spent an embarrassing amount of time on a CORS issue that turned out to be CloudFront silently stripping headers. The fix was a second CloudFront distribution pointing directly to EC2 — but getting there involved a lot of browser console staring.
  - OpenMetadata itself wouldn't run on the EC2 instance I could afford (~4GB RAM required). So I built a proper fallback system — 6 hardcoded fintech demo tables that the real PII scanner runs on. The results are real; only the data source is static.

 What I'll take away isn't the code. It's that building for a real regulatory problem — one where a missed Aadhaar column has an actual penalty attached to it — makes every debugging session feel less abstract. There's a reason to get it right.

Project description:
DataSheriff is an AI-powered data incident investigator that finds the root cause of broken data pipelines in under 30 seconds — instead of the 3–6 hours it typically takes a data engineer manually.

You describe the problem in plain English ("The orders dashboard is showing wrong data") and DataSheriff:

- Searches OpenMetadata for the affected asset
- Traverses the full upstream lineage graph (10+ nodes)
- Checks data quality test results on every table in the chain
- Inspects pipeline execution history for any failed runs
- Identifies the root cause — the first node where tests are actually failing
- Resolves the asset owner so you know who to contact
- Automatically tags the root cause asset as DataQuality.Failing in OpenMetadata for governance tracking
- Streams a structured incident report with every claim backed by a real API call

The investigation runs live in the browser — you watch each tool call happen in real time, a confidence bar climbs from 0% to 100%, and an interactive lineage graph highlights the failing node in red. A history dashboard tracks every past investigation and computes your team's mean time to resolution (MTTR) against the 4.2h industry average.

The app is fully deployed and live at: https://datasheriff.riturajdey01.workers.dev/ 

Demo video: https://youtu.be/FJjLcWuaQ0M
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
DataSheriff is built directly on top of OpenMetadata's REST API — it touches 6 distinct API surfaces in a coordinated, AI-orchestrated investigation loop:

1. Asset Discovery — /api/v1/search/query The investigation starts by searching OpenMetadata for the asset mentioned in the user's plain-English query. This gives back the asset's GUID, fully qualified name, entity type, description, and existing tags.

2. Lineage Traversal — /api/v1/lineage/{entityType}/{id} With the asset ID in hand, DataSheriff fetches the full upstream lineage graph (upstreamDepth=3, downstreamDepth=1). The agent walks every node the API returns — tables, dashboards, pipelines — and never invents hops that OpenMetadata didn't return.

3. Data Quality Tests — /api/v1/dataQuality/testCases For every table node found in lineage, DataSheriff calls the data quality API using the entityLink filter (<#E::table::fqn>). It collects exact test statuses — Success, Failed, Aborted — and their failure messages. This is where root causes are found: the first node with status: Failed becomes the suspect.

4. Pipeline Run History — /api/v1/pipelines/name/{fqn} → /api/v1/pipelines/{id}/status For any pipeline nodes in the lineage graph, DataSheriff resolves the pipeline by FQN to get its ID, then fetches the last 10 execution runs including per-task statuses and failure timestamps.

5. Asset Ownership — /api/v1/{entityType}s/name/{fqn}?fields=owner Once the root cause asset is identified, DataSheriff resolves its owner from OpenMetadata — whether that's an individual user or a team — so the incident report immediately tells you who to contact.

6. Governance Tagging — GET + PATCH /api/v1/{entityType}s/{id} This is the write-back capability that closes the loop. DataSheriff first reads the asset's existing tags, then uses a JSON-Patch request to apply the DataQuality.Failing classification tag. The operation is idempotent — if the tag is already present, it reports that without re-applying. After an investigation, the asset in OpenMetadata itself is annotated and visible under its Tags tab.

The result is a system that doesn't just read from OpenMetadata — it reasons over it and writes back to it, turning OpenMetadata from a passive catalog into an active participant in incident response.
How was your hackathon experience?:
This hackathon pushed me to go much deeper into OpenMetadata than I expected — and that turned out to be the best part of it.

I started thinking I'd build a simple chatbot that queries a few APIs. But once I started actually reading the OpenMetadata documentation and exploring the API surface, I realized how powerful the lineage, quality, and governance APIs really are when used together. The challenge wasn't finding things to do — it was figuring out which combination of APIs would make the most meaningful impact for a real data team.

The hardest technical problem was making the AI agent honest. Claude is very capable, but it will confidently hallucinate lineage paths and test results if you don't constrain it. I ended up writing a detailed system prompt with explicit "Honesty Rules" — the agent is instructed to never invent a node that get_lineage() didn't return, never guess a root cause if tests don't show Failed, and to always produce a null field over a fabricated one. Getting that behavior right and reliable took most of my debugging time.

The OpenMetadata sample data and Airflow integration turned out to be a great starting point — having real failing quality tests in dim_address gave me a genuine end-to-end story to demo, not a mocked-up one.

Overall it was a fantastic experience. Building something that goes from "plain English" to "tagged asset in OpenMetadata" in 30 seconds — with every step visible in real time — felt genuinely useful, not just technically interesting.

Project description:
Every data team dies the same three deaths. Dashboards break and nobody knows why. Schema changes ship and three things break in prod. PII columns lose owners and nobody notices for a quarter. OpenMetadata already knows all of this. It is missing the product surface that lets humans and agents travel between past, present, and future in conversation.

OUTATIME fills that gap with four pillars on one OpenMetadata graph. Past is a Time Machine that bisects change events to root-cause an incident. Present is an Agent Mesh of five specialists with typed tools wired into OpenMetadata's REST APIs. Future is the Flux Capacitor, a deterministic blast-radius simulator with a fully interactive lineage graph. Mirror is a Temporal Diff between any two timestamps.

We use eight OpenMetadata APIs and we ship our own MCP server with nine tools so Claude Desktop, Cursor, and any MCP client can drive OpenMetadata through OUTATIME's time-travel lens.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
OUTATIME treats OpenMetadata as a point-in-time reconstructible knowledge graph and builds four product pillars on top of it. Every pillar reads from the same OpenMetadata graph.

Eight OpenMetadata APIs we read from:

1. Entity APIs for tables, dashboards, dbt models, and ML features. Powers the catalog, the source toggle in the top bar (seeded vs live), and every agent tool surface.
2. Lineage API for upstream and downstream traversal. The Flux Capacitor walks this graph to compute blast radius. Our MCP server exposes it as get_lineage_downstream and get_lineage_upstream.
3. Owners API to resolve who owns each entity. The Sheriff agent flags unowned PII. The Diplomat agent picks who to ping for a schema change. The detail panel in the interactive lineage graph shows owner cards.
4. Tags and Classifications API for PII labels (sensitive, restricted), tier-1 marks, and glossary tags. The Sheriff persona reads these directly to score governance risk.
5. Data Quality API for test status, freshness, and SLA breaches. The Mechanic persona surfaces failing tests. The Past page bisects DQ flips alongside schema events.
6. Versioning and Events API for the full chronological change log. This is the most important API for OUTATIME. The Time Machine bisect, the Mirror diff, and the recent activity feed all replay this log.
7. MCP server (consumed) so each persona in the Agent Mesh has typed tools that route through MCP, not raw REST.
8. Docker stack (docker-compose.openmetadata.yml) plus a seed script (scripts/seed-openmetadata.mjs) that imports our seed graph into a real OpenMetadata instance over REST.

On top of that we ship our own MCP server with nine tools (describe_entity, get_lineage_downstream, get_lineage_upstream, list_dq_failures, list_pii_columns, find_deprecation_candidates, travel_to_iso, bisect_metric, simulate_change) so Claude Desktop, Cursor, Claude Code, and Windsurf can drive OpenMetadata through OUTATIME's time-travel lens without ever opening our UI.

The one-line summary: most teams use one OpenMetadata API. We use eight, plus the MCP surface, plus we expose our own MCP server with nine more tools.
How was your hackathon experience?:
Best part: OpenMetadata's API surface is rich enough that a single builder can wire eight APIs together in a couple of weeks and have something that looks and feels like a real platform tool. The MCP angle especially. The fact that OpenMetadata speaks MCP made the agent mesh almost trivial to wire up, and exposing our own MCP server on top felt like a natural extension rather than an afterthought.

What worked well: the WeMakeDevs Discord was responsive, the project board gave a clear menu of ideas without forcing them, and "original ideas welcome" was a green light I needed.

What I would love next time: an optional Slack/Discord channel paired specifically with the OpenMetadata core team for quick API questions during build week.

Overall, ten out of ten. Built something I will keep using after the deadline. Thanks to the WeMakeDevs and Collate teams for putting this together.

Project description:
Lighthouse turns OpenMetadata into a visual diagnostic console. Three
workflows every data team runs every week — figuring out why a metric
drifted, finding out what breaks if they change a fact table, and
onboarding a new engineer to a domain — currently take about an hour
each. Lighthouse answers all three in under thirty seconds.

The lineage graph is treated as the primary output, not a side panel.
Pick a question, pick an entity, and you get a highlighted lineage
graph, ranked cause cards bound to nodes on that graph, and a
narrative footnoted with clickable links back to the live OpenMetadata
sandbox. After diagnosing, a Suggested Actions panel surfaces
one-click remediations that write back to OpenMetadata: re-trigger an
ingestion DAG, tag a suspect entity, post an announcement banner, or
queue a data-quality rerun.

Lighthouse is read-only by default. Writes are scoped to four
endpoints and only fire when the user explicitly clicks Execute. Demo
mode replays captured fixtures, so the full experience works even
without a sandbox token.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
Lighthouse exercises a deliberately broad slice of the OpenMetadata
API surface — eleven read endpoints plus four scoped write endpoints,
across table, database, databaseSchema, user, glossaryTerm,
ingestionPipeline, and testCase entity types.

Reads do the diagnostic work: lineage traversal at depth three is the
workhorse, table metadata enrichment for every node we visit (owners,
tags, columns, joins), profiling history and data-quality test status
to detect anomalies, glossary terms for the onboarding briefing,
multi-index semantic search for the entity picker, owner lookup for
notifications, and ingestion-pipeline discovery to find triggerable
DAGs.

Writes are user-gated and exposed only through the Suggested Actions
panel. We POST a feed announcement to surface an investigation banner
on a target entity, PATCH a tag onto a suspect via JSON Patch, POST
to the ingestion-pipeline trigger endpoint to re-run an Airflow DAG,
and POST a queued test-case result to record a fresh DQ rerun.

Every endpoint wrapper in the code has a comment with the exact path,
validated against the live sandbox. We probed write capabilities
empirically before exposing them — the resulting capability matrix is
documented in DECISIONS.md.
How was your hackathon experience?:
Genuinely fun. The OpenMetadata sandbox is well-documented and
forgiving, which let us spend our time on the product instead of
fighting auth or schema drift. Picking a single shared demo entity
that worked across all three investigations took longer than expected
— we wrote a small exploration script that ranked tables by lineage
richness, which paid off later when capturing demo fixtures.

The most interesting moment was mid-build: we'd assumed the sandbox
was strictly read-only, but a quick capability probe revealed PATCH
on tables, ingestion-pipeline triggers, and feed posts all worked. We
turned that discovery into the Suggested Actions feature — diagnose
and act in the same console — which became the differentiator we
hadn't planned for.

Honest gaps along the way: profiling history is sparse on most
sandbox tables, so we degrade gracefully and say so in the UI rather
than fabricating numbers. Documenting those limitations openly felt
better than hiding them.

Thanks to WeMakeDevs and the OpenMetadata team for the sandbox
access and a thoughtfully designed API.

Project description:

Project description:
OpenMetadata Sync — GitHub Action for Metadata CI/CD

Every time a developer updates a dbt model, SQL schema, or JSON Schema 
file, someone has to manually update the data catalog in OpenMetadata. 
This never happens consistently, leading to a stale, unreliable catalog 
that teams can't trust.

OpenMetadata Sync is a plug-and-play GitHub Action that automatically 
syncs metadata from your schema files to OpenMetadata on every Pull 
Request — zero manual effort, always up to date.

How it works:
→ Developer opens a PR changing any schema file (.yml, .sql, .json)
→ GitHub Action triggers automatically
→ Parses changed files to extract table descriptions, column info, tags, owners
→ Diffs extracted metadata against current OpenMetadata state
→ Pushes ONLY what changed via OpenMetadata REST API
→ Posts a formatted summary comment on the PR showing exactly what updated

Key Features:
- Supports 3 file formats: dbt YAML models, SQL CREATE TABLE, JSON Schema
- Smart diffing — only updates what actually changed, no redundant API calls
- Automatic PR comments showing a before/after table of all metadata changes
- Dry-run mode for safe testing without writing to OpenMetadata
- Works with any OpenMetadata instance (local Docker, cloud, sandbox)
- Simple setup — just 5 lines in a workflow file, secrets in GitHub
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
Our project integrates deeply with OpenMetadata in the following ways:

1. REST API — Table Lookup
   We use the OpenMetadata Search API (/api/v1/search/query) and the 
   Tables API (/api/v1/tables/name/{fqn}) to fetch the current state 
   of any table in the catalog, including its description, tags, owner, 
   and all column-level metadata.

2. REST API — Metadata Updates (JSON Patch)
   We use HTTP PATCH with JSON Patch operations on /api/v1/tables/{id} 
   to update table descriptions, owners, and tags, as well as 
   column-level descriptions and tags — all via OpenMetadata's 
   official REST API.
3. Column-Level Metadata
   We read and write column descriptions and classification tags 
   (e.g. PII, PK, FK, SENSITIVE) at the column level — one of 
   OpenMetadata's most powerful governance features.

4. Tag Classification System
   We map tags from schema files to OpenMetadata's Classification 
   system (tagFQN format: Classification.TagName), enabling proper 
   governance tagging through the catalog.

The end result: OpenMetadata becomes the single source of truth that 
automatically reflects the latest schema definitions from the codebase without any manual intervention from the data team.
How was your hackathon experience?:
This hackathon was an incredible learning experience. Coming in, I knew 
Python and GitHub Actions basics, but had zero experience with 
OpenMetadata.

The biggest challenge was understanding OpenMetadata's REST API — 
specifically how tables are looked up using Fully Qualified Names (FQNs), 
how JSON Patch works for partial updates, and how the tag classification 
system maps to governance labels. The API docs and the sandbox environment 
were extremely helpful for figuring this out.

The most satisfying moment was seeing the full pipeline work end-to-end 
for the first time — making a change to a dbt YAML file, watching the 
GitHub Action trigger, and seeing the PR comment appear automatically 
with the exact metadata diff.

I'd love to extend this further with lineage tracking (detecting 
column renames and updating lineage graphs) and adding support for 
dbt sources.yml files. Overall a fantastic hackathon — well organized, 
great prize structure, and a genuinely useful real-world problem to solve.

Project description:
OpenMetadata MCP Server++ — an upstream-PR-ready extension of OpenMetadata's Model Context Protocol layer that transforms it from a minimal CRUD interface into a production-grade toolkit for agentic metadata management.

The problem I started from. OpenMetadata's existing MCP server exposes 12 basic tools (search, get, list) that an LLM can call via Claude Desktop or any MCP-compatible client. When benchmarked against realistic data-engineering prompts ("what breaks if I change this table," "who owns this pipeline," "suggest tests for this schema"), tool-selection accuracy sat at 19.4% — agents called the wrong tool, chained them incorrectly, or failed on edge cases around fully-qualified names and nullable fields. That's not enough to be useful.

What I built. A 24-tool MCP server that hits 100% tool-selection accuracy on the same benchmark:

12 new composite and intelligence tools covering change-impact analysis (downstream blast radius + severity rubric), incident timelines (chronological RCA from lineage + test failures + change events), ownership stewardship (unowned-asset discovery, owner suggestion, draft JSON patches), governance coverage scanning, data-contract generation/application, SQL-driven lineage inference, cost-based asset ranking, and test-case suggestion with referential-integrity awareness.
Observability infrastructure — ToolObserver for structured tool-call tracing, EnvelopeBuilder for consistent response shapes, McpEntityBridge for clean dependency injection — all reusable by any future tool.
mcp-bench — a 62-fixture benchmark harness that measures tool-selection accuracy, tool-call efficiency, and latency against realistic prompts. Supports both deterministic fixture replay and BYOK live-LLM runs (OpenAI-compatible). Generates reproducible baseline vs. current markdown reports.
8 tool-selection bug fixes (F1–F8) discovered through the benchmark: FQN chaining, zero-depth lineage, RCA verbosity, search size/offset clamping, JSON filter validation, filter transparency, null guards, and Entity.clear() repository resets.
Rate limiting, safety guards, and byte-cap truncation on every composite tool so agents can't accidentally pull megabytes of metadata in a single call.
What it measures. 19.4% → 100% tool-selection accuracy on 62 fixtures. Avg tool calls per request: 3.4 → 1.3 (−62%). Avg latency: 45 ms → 2 ms (−96%). 908 passing tests across 46 test files, zero failures.

Bonus: security audit. While working in the repo I ran a security review and documented 111 vulnerabilities — 34 GitHub Actions misuse (pull_request_target + template injection), 46 Java SQL/SPARQL injection, 28 Python SQL injection in the ingestion framework, and 3 XXE in XML parsing — with MITRE CWE classification and remediation code for each class. 110 are inherited from upstream; the 1 fork-introduced issue is self-attributed and already fixed. The findings are being responsibly disclosed via GitHub Security Advisories.

Engineering approach. Every change traces from a fixed scope document through a bench fixture to passing tests before landing in main. The 19.4% → 100% jump is the measurable outcome of that spec-first process.

Status: All changes are backward-compatible and shaped like upstream PRs.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
This project extends OpenMetadata from the inside. The openmetadata-mcp module lives in the same Maven reactor as openmetadata-service, is built by the same mvn test -pl openmetadata-mcp command, and deploys as part of the OpenMetadata server itself. The 24 MCP tools run in-process with direct access to OpenMetadata's EntityRepository, LineageRepository, TestCaseRepository, ChangeEventRepository, and search index — no REST hop, no external adapter, no duplicated state.

APIs. Every write-producing tool emits output that round-trips through OpenMetadata's existing PATCH /v1/<entity> endpoints. draft_ownership_patch returns an RFC 6902 JSON Patch an operator can apply unchanged. apply_data_contract writes through Table.dataContract using OpenMetadata's standard JSON Schema validation. Responses are standardized by a new EnvelopeBuilder that mirrors the shape of existing OpenMetadata REST responses for backward compatibility with any client that already knows the API.

Connectors. Because tools read from EntityRepository directly (via a new McpEntityBridge DI layer), every source OpenMetadata can ingest — Snowflake, Postgres, BigQuery, Redshift, dbt, Airflow, Tableau, Looker, Superset, Kafka, Pulsar, S3, Iceberg, etc. — is instantly addressable through the new MCP tools. No per-source code had to be added: the connector catalog is inherited for free.

Lineage. change_impact traverses the upstream/downstream lineage graph with configurable depth (default 3, capped at 5), returns a compact narrative plus structured results, and applies an 8 KB byte cap with warnings on truncation so agents can't flood context windows. lineage_from_sql parses a SQL statement and emits candidate lineage edges in OpenMetadata's native edge format, ready to merge into the graph. incident_timeline joins lineage edges, ChangeEvent history, and TestCase failures into a single chronologically-ordered RCA narrative — exactly the pattern a human SRE walks when debugging a pipeline.

Governance. A complete stewardship surface built on OpenMetadata's native governance primitives. find_unowned_assets enumerates assets where owners is empty, ranked by downstream impact (using lineage) so the highest-leverage fixes surface first — rate-limited to 5 min/user to prevent catalog-wide scans. suggest_owner_for uses historical ownership + team membership + domain affinity to propose candidates. draft_ownership_patch produces a ready-to-apply JSON Patch. scan_governance_coverage reports on Tags, Tiers, Classifications, Glossary Terms, Descriptions, and Ownership coverage — all first-class OpenMetadata concepts.

Observability. ToolObserver emits structured events for every tool invocation — tool name, inputs, response size, duration, error class — routed through OpenMetadata's existing logging/metrics stack. Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
OpenMetadata is the backbone of MetaLens. We run OpenMetadata locally via Docker and use its REST API to:
1. Store dataset metadata
We register our datasets in OpenMetadata with full column-level detail — data types, descriptions, ownership, and classification tags like PII.Sensitive on columns such as email.
2.Fetch metadata at runtime
When a user uploads an Excel file, MetaLens queries the OpenMetadata API to find the matching dataset and pull its metadata — owner, tags, lineage, and usage context.
3. PII detection via tags
OpenMetadata's tagging system (PII.Sensitive, PII.NonSensitive) is used to automatically flag sensitive columns and warn users before they make changes.
4. Lineage for impact analysis
OpenMetadata's lineage graph tells us where data comes from and where it flows. MetaLens uses this to answer "what breaks if I modify this column?
5. Context for AI
All metadata fetched from OpenMetadata is passed to the AI layer as context. Without OpenMetadata, the AI only sees raw numbers. With it, the AI understands the data's meaning, sensitivity, and business impact.

This was my first time working with a metadata platform, and OpenMetadata genuinely surprised me. Setting it up via Docker, exploring the REST API, and understanding how metadata connects to real data — it was a completely new way of thinking about data for me.

Project description: Pipeline Autopsy is an AI-powered root cause analysis tool for data pipeline failures, built on OpenMetadata. When a pipeline breaks, it automatically traverses the upstream lineage graph, detects the exact schema change that caused the failure, and uses an LLM to explain what broke and why in plain language - along with a suggested fix. It also includes a GitHub PR bot that catches breaking schema changes before they are merged, posting a lineage impact report directly on the pull request.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
I built Pipeline Autopsy around OpenMetadata because I needed a single source of truth for everything happening across my data pipelines - lineage, schema history, asset ownership, all of it in one place.
When a data pipeline breaks, the hardest part is not fixing it - it is figuring out where it broke and why. That is the problem I solved using OpenMetadata as the backbone.
Here is how I actually use it:
Lineage traversal for root cause hunting - When a failure comes in, whether from a dbt webhook, a GitHub PR, or a manual query in my chat UI, I immediately hit OpenMetadata's lineage API to walk upstream from the failing asset. I go up to 3 levels deep, building a dependency graph that shows exactly which tables and models feed into the broken one. This is what lets me pinpoint the origin of the failure rather than just seeing the symptom.
Schema version history for change detection - Once I have the lineage graph, I pull schema version history for each node using OpenMetadata's table versions API. I diff the last two versions to find added, removed, or modified columns. Nine times out of ten, that is the root cause - someone renamed a column upstream and everything downstream quietly broke.
GitHub PR bot powered by lineage - This is where it gets interesting. I hooked OpenMetadata's lineage directly into a GitHub App I built. When a developer opens a PR that touches .sql or .yml files, my bot automatically fetches the lineage subgraph for affected assets from OpenMetadata, runs AI analysis on the impact, and posts a structured comment on the PR before the code is even merged. It tells the developer exactly which downstream assets will break, who owns them, and how to fix it.
The LLM never sees raw data - it sees structured lineage context from OpenMetadata, which is what makes the root cause analysis actually accurate rather than generic AI guessing.
How was your hackathon experience?: Honestly it was one of the more intense building experiences I have had. I came in with the idea of solving something I genuinely found frustrating - when data pipelines break, the debugging process is slow, manual, and scattered across too many tools. I wanted to fix that.The hardest part was getting OpenMetadata's lineage API to behave the way I needed it to. Traversing upstream dependencies recursively, detecting the exact break point, and then packaging all of that as clean context for an LLM took a lot of iteration. There were moments where the AI was giving confident but completely wrong root cause summaries because the context I was feeding it was too noisy.The GitHub PR bot was the part I was most excited to build. The idea that a developer could open a pull request, change a column name in a SQL model, and immediately get a comment telling them exactly which downstream assets will break before anything is merged - that felt like something actually useful, not just a demo.By the end I had a working end to end system - lineage traversal, AI analysis, a chat interface, and the GitHub bot all talking to each other. There is still a lot I want to improve, especially around the schema diff detection and making the bot smarter about what counts as a breaking change.Overall it pushed me to go deeper on data engineering tooling than I expected, and I walked away with something I actually want to keep building.

Project description:
SwaggerLens: AI-Powered API Discovery & Governance Pipeline Modern engineering teams deploy thousands of API endpoints, but maintaining accurate OpenAPI (Swagger) documentation is almost always a manual, neglected chore. This leads to "Shadow APIs", where security teams lose visibility of what is running, and engineering teams waste time guessing how undocumented services work.

SwaggerLens is an end-to-end pipeline that solves this by generating 100% accurate API documentation autonomously—based purely on the actual traffic your application receives. Our architecture accomplishes this in three steps:

1. Discovery: It analyzes incoming server logs (Nginx, Spring Boot, Elasticsearch), normalizing dynamic routes and extracting active HTTP execution patterns.
2. AI Generation: It passes these raw logs through Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash LLM, converting unstructured traffic data into beautifully formatted, strictly validated OpenAPI 3.0.3 specifications.
3. Governance: Finally, it takes that raw specification and pushes it directly into the OpenMetadata platform natively, transforming a static file into a globally categorized, searchable data asset.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
Instead of treating OpenMetadata just as a static catalog, we used it as the central nervous system for organizational API governance. In our project, OpenMetadata is the ultimate destination for our AI-generated API intelligence.

We built a custom Python integration layer that directly communicates with OpenMetadata's REST APIs. When SwaggerLens identifies a new service from server logs, it programmatically injects a payload into OpenMetadata that recursively provisions the entire architectural tree:

It creates a dedicated API Service within the OpenMetadata interface.
It nests a comprehensive API Collection underneath it.
It maps every single individual route (e.g., GET /users/{id}) as an explicit API Endpoint asset.
By doing this, we turned OpenMetadata into an automated API Security and Discovery hub. Without a developer writing a single line of YAML, operations teams can now log into OpenMetadata and see a fully cataloged list of every endpoint actually functioning in production, complete with descriptions, methods, and searchability.
How was your hackathon experience?:
This hackathon was exceptionally rewarding and pushed our technical boundaries in the best way possible! The "aha" moment of the event was seeing our unstructured server traffic logs successfully convert into a beautifully governed catalog asset inside the OpenMetadata UI for the very first time.

Working with OpenMetadata wasn't just about plugging in an API; it required us to genuinely understand the metadata ingestion framework, rigorous schema validations, and exactly how data assets are structured inside the platform (down to the java.net.URI serialization constraints!). Building a bridge between infrastructure logs, Artificial Intelligence, and enterprise Data Governance was challenging, but the ecosystem OpenMetadata provides made building an enterprise-grade solution incredibly fluid. It was an amazing learning experience!

Project description:
OpenBlame is a local-first AI investigation CLI for data pipelines running on OpenMetadata. Point it to a table, and it will trace lineage, inspect recent quality failures, parse schema-changes, surface governance gaps, and draft a root-cause narrative.

The reasoning layer runs entirely on your local Ollama models, ensuring your metadata stays inside your environment.

Autonomous Investigation: ReAct-style agent loop that plans and executes metadata research.
Lineage & Blast Radius: Automatic upstream/downstream analysis to find affected entities.
Schema Drift: Instant diffing of column changes, type updates, and renames.
Governance Aware: Surfaces missing owners, tiers, and domain gaps as operational risks.
Local-First AI: Powered by Ollama (qwen2.5, llama3, etc.). No external API keys needed for reasoning.
MCP Ready: Built-in Model Context Protocol server to integrate with AI IDEs like Cursor and Claude Desktop.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
OpenBlame is built entirely on top of OpenMetadata as its single source of truth. We do not store any metadata ourselves — every piece of data the agent reasons over comes directly from OpenMetadata's REST API in real time.

Lineage — We call `GET /api/v1/lineage/table/name/{fqn}` with configurable upstream and downstream depth. The agent parses the node and edge graph to identify which tables are the upstream root cause of an incident and which downstream consumers are impacted. This gives the blast radius — something that previously required a data engineer to trace manually.

Data Quality — We call `GET /api/v1/dataQuality/testCases` filtered by entity link and a configurable day lookback window. The agent extracts failed tests with column-level precision, timestamps, expected versus actual values, and failure messages. Quality failures are a primary signal in the incident report.

Schema History — We call `GET /api/v1/tables/name/{fqn}` for the current column definition, and `GET /api/v1/feed?type=EntityUpdated` for the change event feed. The agent parses field-level change events to detect column additions, removals, and type changes — with the timestamp and the user who made the change. A type change like FLOAT(2) to FLOAT(4) three days ago is often the exact root cause of a broken downstream metric.

Governance and Ownership — We call `GET /api/v1/tables/name/{fqn}?fields=owners,tags,domain,extension` to surface the table's owners, tier classification, domain, tags, and description. Missing owner, missing tier, or missing tags are treated as operational risk signals — not just metadata gaps — and are explicitly called out in the severity assessment.

All four API calls run in parallel using asyncio, and every call is wrapped in graceful error handling — if OpenMetadata is slow or a particular endpoint returns nothing, the agent continues with partial data and notes the gap in the report.

The Ollama LLM then reasons over the combined evidence from all four surfaces and produces a structured incident report — root cause, impact, evidence, owner, suggested fix, and severity level — entirely grounded in what OpenMetadata knows about that table.

We also expose the agent as an MCP server with three tools — `investigate_table`, `get_lineage`, and `get_schema_diff` — so OpenMetadata's metadata becomes queryable from any MCP-compatible client like Claude or Cursor.

Project description:
ChaosMetadata is a chaos engineering tool designed specifically for your data catalog, built for the WeMakeDevs × OpenMetadata Hackathon. It allows data teams to deliberately inject simulated failures into their data infrastructure directly from Slack. The core goal is to prove whether your organization's data observability, alerting, and governance practices actually work during an incident.

The Problem It Solves
Most data teams only discover that their observability is broken during a real incident, leading to corrupted dashboards, broken ML models, and lost trust. ChaosMetadata addresses this by allowing you to proactively test your systems with controlled "experiments" to see if your detection mechanisms trigger as expected.

Key Features
Zero Real-Data Risk: Experiments happen strictly at the metadata layer. It tests your detection capabilities, not whether your data physically survives the event.
Blast Radius Analysis: Before executing an experiment, the tool computes the impact using the OpenMetadata lineage graph (e.g., "3 dashboards, 1 ML model will be affected").
Multiple Experiment Types:
row-drop: Simulates rows disappearing to test row count monitoring.
schema-change: Simulates dropped critical columns to test schema change detection.
null-flood: Simulates spikes in NULL values to test data quality alerts.
freshness: Simulates stale tables to test freshness monitoring.
ownership-gap & pii-exposure: Tests governance and auto-classification alerting.
Resilience Scoring: Generates a platform resilience score out of 100 based on Detection Speed (30%), Alert Reliability (35%), Ownership Coverage (20%), and Response Time (15%).
Seamless Slack Integration: Entirely controllable via Slack slash commands (/chaos run, /chaos preview, /chaos score, etc.) using Slack Socket Mode, meaning it requires zero complex infrastructure to run.

Architecture & Tech Stack
Backend: Go (Golang) handling the chaos runner, OpenMetadata API client, BFS lineage traversal, and the Slack handler.
Data Catalog: OpenMetadata (Docker) for metadata operations, lineage, and search.
Connectivity: Slack Socket Mode (free, fast, and secure).
AI/ML: Local LLM integration via Ollama + Llama 3 for anomaly detection and PII detection.

ChaosMetadata provides a continuous feedback loop for data engineers to build trust in their data platform by treating failure as an expected and testable event.

Lineage API: We use it to calculate the "blast radius" of our simulated failures, instantly showing users which downstream dashboards and ML models will break.
Incidents & Governance APIs: We inject our chaos experiments directly into OpenMetadata (by creating P1 incidents and tagging tables) to test if the team's alerts fire, without ever risking real data.
Search API: We integrated this into our Slack bot so users can find and target tables for experiments natively in Slack.
Resilience Scoring: We query OpenMetadata's existing metadata to calculate a company's "Resilience Score," exposing governance gaps like tables that are missing owners or tiering.

Project description:
We've made a production-ready GitHub Action for data impact analysis. Its purpose is to help teams understand how a pull request could affect downstream data assets before changes are merged. When a PR modifies SQL, dbt, or schema-related files, the action identifies the changed data objects, looks up their lineage in OpenMetadata, and calculates what dashboards, pipelines, reports, tables, views, topics, and other assets could be impacted.

The action is designed for real CI use, not just a demo. It runs on pull request events, reads the PR diff, filters for tracked data files, extracts changed entities, normalizes them into canonical names, and then traverses downstream lineage with guardrails such as depth limits, concurrency limits, entity caps, and downstream asset caps. It can talk to OpenMetadata in three modes: direct API mode, MCP mode, or auto mode, where MCP is tried first and the API is used as a fallback if MCP is incomplete or unavailable. It also handles different OpenMetadata lineage response shapes across versions.

The output is meant to be immediately useful to reviewers and automation. The action publishes a PR comment with a summary of the impact, impacted assets grouped by type, warnings, and suggestions. It also writes a GitHub Actions job summary and exposes machine-readable outputs such as risk level, impacted asset count, warning counts, analysis status, retry metrics, and structured JSON for follow-up workflow steps. Risk is determined by a combination of blast radius, warning thresholds, low-confidence extraction, critical tags, and optional weighted governance signals.

The project also includes strong operational and security controls. It validates endpoints, restricts unsafe network access by default, supports secure token handling, masks secrets, and sanitizes comment output to avoid unsafe markdown behavior. It is built in TypeScript for Node 24, bundled for GitHub Actions, and supported by CI, CodeQL, secret scanning, release automation, and OpenMetadata compatibility tests. 

In practice, it is a complete PR-based data governance workflow that tells reviewers how risky a data change is and what downstream systems they should pay attention to.

OpenMetadata is the project’s source of truth for data lineage and governance when a pull request changes SQL, dbt, or schema files. We support two ways of talking to OpenMetadata. In normal API mode, the action calls the documented lineage endpoint directly and walks the downstream graph to a limited depth. In MCP mode, it uses OpenMetadata’s MCP JSON-RPC tools instead. There is also an auto mode that prefers MCP first and falls back to the API if MCP is partial, unavailable, or returns incomplete results.

OpenMetadata data is also used to enrich and judge impact, not just to list lineage. The action pulls metadata like owners, domains, tags, and glossary terms, then uses that context to raise risk for critical assets and to generate a PR comment, GitHub Actions summary, and machine-readable outputs. The implementation is designed to handle multiple OpenMetadata response shapes and service conditions, so it can work across different OpenMetadata versions and deployments.

Project description:

It moves beyond passive metadata cataloging by automatically computing a dynamic "Trust Score" (0-100) for every table in the platform, answering the critical question: "Can I trust this data right now?"

The engine deeply integrates with OpenMetadata's APIs, leveraging: Profiler API Integration: Instead of just counting tests, it natively parses OpenMetadata's row-level statistics, column null-proportions, and profiling coverage.

Lineage-Based Trust Propagation: It doesn't just score a table in isolation. The engine uses OpenMetadata's Lineage API to traverse the upstream graph. If a source table loses an owner or starts failing tests, that risk automatically propagates down to all consumer tables.

Webhook Subscriptions (Event-Driven): Instead of slow batch polling, the engine registers an OmEventSubscriber via OpenMetadata's Webhook API. When metadata changes (e.g., an owner is added, a description is updated), OpenMetadata pings the engine, triggering an instant, targeted rescore.

Actionable Recommendations Engine: The dashboard identifies governance gaps and computes "Fix First" recommendations (e.g., "Assign an owner: +25 pts"), turning metadata hygiene into a gamified, actionable workflow.

JSON Patching: Every scoring cycle, my Java backend calculates reliability scores and writes them back into OpenMetadata's native UI via JSON Patch requests.

Project description:
AI-Powered Compliance & Breach Impact Agent for OpenMetadata
Stop guessing. Start knowing. Protect what matters.

DataGuardian is a production-ready MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that transforms your OpenMetadata catalog into an always-on compliance analyst — discovering sensitive data, mapping breach blast radius, enforcing governance, and generating incident playbooks in seconds, all through natural language.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
How I Used OpenMetadata:

DataGuardian is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that turns OpenMetadata into an always-on AI compliance analyst. The entire project is built around OpenMetadata's REST API — it's not just an integration, it's the core data layer the agent reasons over.

Here's specifically how OpenMetadata is used across the eleven tools:

Asset Discovery via Search API The search_sensitive tool queries /api/v1/search/query using tags.tagFQN:<tag> against OpenMetadata's unified search index to find assets tagged PII, GDPR, HIPAA, PHI, Sensitive, or Confidential. This powers the compliance inventory, orphan detection, bulk classification, and retention checking tools.

Lineage Graph Traversal The breach_impact tool implements a BFS traversal over OpenMetadata's lineage graph using /api/v1/lineage/{type}/{id}. Starting from any asset FQN, it walks downstream (or upstream) edges up to a configurable depth to compute the full blast radius of a data breach — which tables, dashboards, pipelines, and ML models are affected.

Schema Inspection and Tag Write-Back The classify_table tool fetches a table's full schema from /api/v1/tables/name/{fqn}, sends column names and types to Gemini for PII detection, then writes the detected tags back to OpenMetadata using RFC 6902 JSON Patch (PATCH /api/v1/tables/{id}). Project description:
I built MetaFlow — an AI agent that sits on top of OpenMetadata and actually does things, not just answers questions about data.
The problem I kept running into: you have a data catalog full of useful metadata, but when something breaks — a table fails a quality check, a schema drifts, a contract gets violated — someone still has to manually open Jira, post to Slack, email the data owner, and patch the health score back into the catalog. That's four tools, four browser tabs, and usually gets skipped at 2am.
MetaFlow automates that whole loop. You describe the incident once, and it routes to the right specialist agents — GitHub for the ticket, Slack for the alert, Jira for the task, Notion for the log, email for the data owner. All carrying the actual metadata context from OpenMetadata: the table FQN, the failing contract gate, the SQL fix. It also writes a health score back into OpenMetadata as a native custom property, which I think is the part most catalog tools skip — they read metadata, but never write it back.
Under the hood it's a LangGraph supervisor with 5 specialist agents, 15 pre-built incident playbooks, a continuous data steward that monitors events in the background, and a Contract Copilot that generates and publishes native OpenMetadata data contracts with real test gates.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
Pretty much as the source of truth for everything.
The steward polls OpenMetadata's test result events to detect DQ failures in real time. The Contract Copilot calls the OpenMetadata API to fetch table columns, infers quality gates from the schema, then publishes a real data contract back via the /api/v1/dataContracts endpoint — not a MetaFlow concept, an actual OpenMetadata object that shows up in the native UI.
The governance agent reads completeness, PII tags, and lineage from OpenMetadata, computes a health score, and PATCHes it back as a custom property (metaflow_health_score) on the table entity. Refresh the page in OpenMetadata's own UI and it's there. Any user on the instance sees it.
The impact radar pulls upstream/downstream lineage from OpenMetadata to show which assets are at risk when a table fails. The cause tree maps test failures back to the originating table using the same lineage data.
Basically every agent action starts and ends with OpenMetadata — read the context, do the work, write back the result.
How was your hackathon experience?:
Honestly pretty chaotic but in a good way.
I started with a clear idea — make OpenMetadata agentic — but underestimated how much the "write-back" part would take. Most of the LLM + metadata integrations I found online are read-only. Getting agents to actually mutate catalog state, not just query it, required a lot more trial and error than I expected.
The free API key rate limits were a real constraint. Gemini's free tier is generous but when you have a LangGraph supervisor routing to specialists, each message is 6-8 LLM calls. I hit 429s constantly early on and had to build a rotating key pool and retry logic just to get a stable demo.
The thing I'm most proud of is the Contract Copilot + governance write-back combination — it felt like the point where it stopped being a chatbot wrapper and started being an actual data engineering tool. That part took the longest to get right but it's also the most defensible thing in the submission.
Would have loved more time to harden the playbooks and clean up the UI, but given the timeline I think it covers a lot of real ground.

Kestra is one of the fastest-growing open-source orchestrators, and a real chunk of modern data teams run on it. OpenMetadata's MCP server today can describe the catalog beautifully, but the moment something breaks, it falls silent: it can't run anything, it can't check anything, it can't set anything up. So when a pipeline fails at 2am, the assistant becomes a bystander. I added three actions that turn that around: trigger a run, check the last few runs, set up an alert on future failures. Now the entire incident loop ("did the ETL run last night? run it again. alert me if it fails next time.") happens in a single Claude conversation, without the user ever opening Airflow, Slack, or the OpenMetadata UI. Both contributions follow the same theme: meet users where they already are. The Kestra connector meets a community OpenMetadata wasn't reaching yet.
