Project description:
Neo Catalog
An AI-powered Data Intelligence Assistant that brings natural language understanding to your data catalog — built on OpenMetadata, powered by Gemini 2.0 Flash.

The problem

Data teams spend hours navigating complex metadata catalogs just to answer basic questions — who owns this table? what does this field mean? is this data fresh? These answers exist in your catalog, but they're buried behind UIs that require expertise to navigate. Neo Catalog removes that friction entirely.

What we built

Neo Catalog is a conversational AI layer on top of OpenMetadata. Users type questions in plain English and get instant, structured answers — with direct links back to the catalog UI. Under the hood, Gemini 2.0 Flash drives a real-time tool-calling loop that queries live OpenMetadata APIs across eight distinct capabilities.

Key capabilities

Catalog search

Natural language queries across tables, dashboards, and pipelines

Schema inspection

Column metadata, data types, and tags on demand

Lineage tracing

Upstream and downstream data dependency graphs

DQ checks

Data quality test results per table, conversationally accessible

Notion logging

Log governance issues directly to Notion databases from chat

Business glossary

Bridge technical assets to business definitions instantly

How it works

1
User asks a question

"Show me the schema for the orders table and check its data quality."

2
Intent detection

A lightweight router classifies the task and passes it to the Gemini function-call loop.

3
Tool-calling loop (max 5 turns)

Gemini 2.0 Flash selects and calls the right OpenMetadata API tools — up to 8 distinct capabilities.

4
Structured response + catalog link

Every answer includes a direct clickable link to the relevant asset in the OpenMetadata UI.

Tech stack

Next.js 15 (App Router)
TypeScript
Gemini 2.0 Flash
OpenMetadata REST API
Tailwind CSS 4
Notion API
Google Cloud Run
What makes it stand out

Multi-model fallback
Auto-switches to Gemini 1.5 Flash on quota limits — zero downtime for end users.

Multi-turn conversations
Full conversational context is maintained across turns, enabling deep follow-up queries.

Production-ready
Ships with a multi-stage Dockerfile and one-command Cloud Run deployment out of the box.

Governance-first
DQ issues can be logged to Notion directly from the chat — keeping governance workflows in sync.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
OpenMetadata as the Core Data Backbone
Neo Catalog doesn't just integrate with OpenMetadata — it is entirely powered by it. OpenMetadata serves as the single source of truth for all data intelligence in the application. Every answer Neo Catalog gives originates from a live OpenMetadata API call, never from cached or static data.

1. REST API Client (lib/om-client.ts)
A dedicated OpenMetadata REST API client was built to act as the bridge between the AI layer and the catalog. It handles authentication via a JWT token, constructs properly scoped API requests, and parses structured responses back to the tool executor. This client is the engine behind every catalog interaction.

2. The 8 OpenMetadata-Powered Tools
Every tool in Neo Catalog maps directly to a specific OpenMetadata API endpoint:
ToolOpenMetadata Usagesearch_assetsFull-text search across tables, dashboards, topics, and pipelines using OpenMetadata's search APIget_table_schemaFetches column-level metadata — names, data types, descriptions, and tags — for any tableget_lineageRetrieves upstream and downstream lineage graphs, showing data dependencies across assetslist_dq_checksPulls data quality test definitions and their latest results for a given tableget_table_profileFetches profiling metadata — row counts, storage size, null percentages, and freshness timestampssearch_peopleQueries OpenMetadata's Teams & Users API to find table owners and responsible teamssearch_glossaryLooks up business glossary terms to map technical assets to business definitionsget_sample_dataRetrieves sample row data stored against a table in the catalog

3. Real-Time, Not Cached
A deliberate architectural decision was made to call OpenMetadata APIs live on every query. There is no intermediate database or cache layer. This ensures that schema changes, freshness timestamps, DQ results, and ownership data are always current — which is critical for a data governance tool.

4. Direct Catalog Links in Every Response
Every response Neo Catalog generates includes a clickable deep link back to the relevant asset in the OpenMetadata UI. This was built by constructing asset URLs from the OM_HOST environment variable combined with the asset's fully qualified name (FQN) returned by the API. Users can go from a conversational answer directly into the catalog in one click.

5. Fully Qualified Name (FQN) as the Universal Asset Identifier
OpenMetadata's FQN system (e.g., sample_data.ecommerce_db.shopify.orders) is used throughout Neo Catalog as the canonical identifier for every asset. The router and tool executor both rely on FQNs to scope API calls correctly, ensuring the right asset is retrieved even across multiple databases or services within the same OpenMetadata instance.

6. Authentication
Neo Catalog authenticates with OpenMetadata using a JWT Bearer token passed via the OM_TOKEN environment variable. The om-client.ts sets this token on every outbound request header, making it compatible with any OpenMetadata instance — the public sandbox, a self-hosted deployment, or a managed cloud version.

Summary
OpenMetadata is not a peripheral integration in Neo Catalog — it is the foundation. The AI layer (Gemini) acts as an intelligent interface on top of it, but every piece of data, every schema, every lineage graph, every quality check, and every ownership record comes directly from OpenMetadata's APIs in real time.
How was your hackathon experience?:
Building Neo Catalog
From idea to deployed product — the journey of building an AI-powered data intelligence assistant in a single hackathon sprint.

The spark

The idea for Neo Catalog came from a real frustration — navigating OpenMetadata to answer even simple questions like "who owns this table?" or "is this data fresh?" required clicking through multiple UI screens. The hackathon felt like the perfect forcing function to ask: what if you could just ask in plain English? That single question became the entire project.

The journey

1
Exploring OpenMetadata's API surface

The first hours were spent deep in OpenMetadata's REST API docs — understanding the search endpoints, FQN structure, lineage graph format, and how DQ checks are stored. This exploration directly shaped the 8 tools that Neo Catalog exposes to Gemini.

2
Designing the tool-calling architecture

The core architectural decision was to not have Gemini call APIs directly, but to build a tool executor layer — a clean mapping of function names to typed OpenMetadata calls. This made the AI layer swappable and kept the catalog logic testable and isolated.

3
The Gemini function-call loop challenge

Getting Gemini to reliably select the right tool — and chain multiple tools for compound queries — required significant prompt iteration. The max-5-turn loop was a deliberate cap to keep responses fast while still handling complex multi-step questions like "show me the schema and then check its quality."

4
Hitting quota limits — and solving it in real time

During testing, Gemini 2.0 Flash started hitting rate limits under heavy load. Rather than accepting downtime, a multi-model fallback was implemented that transparently switches to Gemini 1.5 Flash when quota is exceeded — an unplanned feature that became one of the project's strongest reliability stories.

5
Adding Notion logging — a late pivot

Notion integration wasn't in the original plan. Midway through the hackathon, it became clear that a governance tool should close the loop — not just surface issues but log them. The Notion logger was built in a focused sprint and added a meaningful workflow dimension to what was otherwise a read-only tool.

6
Deploying to Cloud Run

The final push was making Neo Catalog genuinely deployable, not just a localhost demo. A multi-stage Dockerfile was written, Next.js was configured for standalone output, and a one-command Cloud Run deployment was tested end-to-end before submission.

Biggest challenges

Taming multi-turn tool chaining

Getting Gemini to correctly resolve ambiguous queries into a clean sequence of tool calls — without hallucinating asset names or FQNs — required careful system prompt design and extensive testing against the OpenMetadata sandbox.

OpenMetadata response normalization

Different OpenMetadata API endpoints return data in inconsistent shapes. The `om-client.ts` had to normalize these responses into a consistent structure before handing them to Gemini — otherwise the model would trip over missing fields or unexpected nesting.

Keeping response latency acceptable

A multi-turn AI loop over live APIs can be slow. Balancing the depth of tool calls against response time — and deciding when one API call is enough vs. when to chain — was an ongoing tradeoff throughout the build.

What we learned

APIs as AI tools

Any well-documented REST API can become an AI tool with the right abstraction layer — the hard part is normalization, not the AI.

Resilience matters

The multi-model fallback wasn't planned — but solving a real problem under pressure produced the project's most robust feature.

Ship real deployments

Taking the time to write a proper Dockerfile and test Cloud Run made the project credible as a real product, not just a hackathon demo.

What's next

Neo Catalog proved that a conversational interface over a data catalog is genuinely useful — not just a novelty. The next steps would be adding streaming responses for perceived speed, expanding to more catalog platforms beyond OpenMetadata, and building a richer governance workflow with two-way Notion sync.

Project description: FLUX is an autonomous temporal lineage steward for OpenMetadata. It snapshots your lineage graph, computes temporal diffs against prior state, classifies breaks (schema drift, PII orphan, ghost edge) in under a second using deterministic rules, and autonomously heals low-risk issues while queueing high-risk decisions for human review with full audit trails. Built with Python 3.10+, Pydantic v2, NetworkX.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
OpenMetadata is the foundational platform that FLUX monitors, protects, and heals. We use it in three dimensions:

1. As the Source of Truth: FLUX consumes OpenMetadata's REST API (via httpx with JWT authentication) to fetch full lineage graphs, table schemas, column metadata, tags, owners, and descriptions. We leverage the /v1/lineage/table/{id} endpoint with configurable upstream/downstream depth to build complete temporal snapshots stored as JSON fingerprints.

2. As the Break Detection Surface: We compare current OM state (Tn) against prior snapshots (T0) to detect temporal breaks — added/removed lineage edges, column renames, type changes, missing PII tags, and ownership voids. OpenMetadata's structured entity model (tables, schemas, columns, tags) gives us the granular metadata needed for deterministic classification.

3. As the Healing Target: FLUX writes back all remediation actions directly into OpenMetadata. We use JSON Patch to add PII.Email tags to columns, update table descriptions with [FLUX AUTO-NOTE] annotations documenting detected breaks, append [FLUX REVIEW QUEUE] notes for human-reviewed actions, and create lineage edges. This makes OM itself the living audit trail — every heal action is visible to data consumers browsing the catalog.
How was your hackathon experience?: Brutal, then exhilarating. I burned half a day fighting OpenMetadata JSON Patch headers and team ownership rules, then hit a wall when Fireworks.ai GLM-5.1 took 10 minutes per call. The breakthrough was pivoting to a hybrid architecture: deterministic rules for speed (<3 sec), AI mode as an optional flag. The payoff was the live demo — watching FLUX trace a rename → PII orphan → blast radius → cascade heal across three teams in one terminal tree. That single output made the entire hackathon worth it.

Pretty much as the source of truth for everything.
The steward polls OpenMetadata's test result events to detect DQ failures in real time. The Contract Copilot calls the OpenMetadata API to fetch table columns, infers quality gates from the schema, then publishes a real data contract back via the /api/v1/dataContracts endpoint — not a MetaFlow concept, an actual OpenMetadata object that shows up in the native UI.
The governance agent reads completeness, PII tags, and lineage from OpenMetadata, computes a health score, and PATCHes it back as a custom property (metaflow_health_score) on the table entity. Refresh the page in OpenMetadata's own UI and it's there. Any user on the instance sees it.
The impact radar pulls upstream/downstream lineage from OpenMetadata to show which assets are at risk when a table fails. The cause tree maps test failures back to the originating table using the same lineage data.
Basically every agent action starts and ends with OpenMetadata — read the context, do the work, write back the result.
How was your hackathon experience?:
Honestly pretty chaotic but in a good way.
I started with a clear idea — make OpenMetadata agentic — but underestimated how much the "write-back" part would take. Most of the LLM + metadata integrations I found online are read-only. The free API key rate limits were a real constraint. Gemini's free tier is generous but when you have a LangGraph supervisor routing to specialists, each message is 6-8 LLM calls. I hit 429s constantly early on and had to build a rotating key pool and retry logic just to get a stable demo.
The thing I'm most proud of is the Contract Copilot + governance write-back combination — it felt like the point where it stopped being a chatbot wrapper and started being an actual data engineering tool. That part took the longest to get right but it's also the most defensible thing in the submission.

Project description:
Incidere is a proactive data incident response agent that turns OpenMetadata from a passive data catalog into an active incident responder. When a data quality issue is detected (null rate spikes, schema drift, pipeline failures), Incidere queries OpenMetadata's REST API for entity details, lineage graphs, downstream impact, and ownership which then classifies severity based on anomaly type and blast radius, calls the on-call engineer via ElevenLabs AI voice + Twilio, and posts structured Block Kit reports to Slack.

Built as an MCP server with 11 tools (5 OpenMetadata tools, 4 Slack tools, 2 orchestrator tools), deployed on Vercel via xmcp framework. Tested against the live OpenMetadata sandbox with real data — dim_customers table with 12 columns, 4 lineage nodes, 2 downstream entities, owner nick.acosta.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
Incidere integrates deeply with OpenMetadata's REST API through 5 dedicated MCP tools:

1. search-metadata — Calls GET /v1/search/query with Elasticsearch syntax to search entities by keyword, filtered by entity type (table, pipeline, dashboard). Supports the fields parameter for including columns, owners, tags.

2. get-entity-details — Calls GET /v1/tables/name/{fqn}?fields=owners,tags,columns to retrieve full entity details including schema, ownership, tags, and tier classification.

3. get-entity-lineage — Calls GET /v1/lineage/table/name/{fqn}?upstreamDepth=3&downstreamDepth=3 to retrieve the full lineage graph with upstream and downstream edges, column-level lineage, and pipeline references.

4. get-entity-owners — Extracts ownership information from entity metadata to identify the on-call engineer for phone call routing.

5. assess-downstream-impact — Performs BFS traversal of the downstream lineage graph using entity UUIDs from edge references, categorizing impacted entities into tables, dashboards, and pipelines with depth tracking.

The severity classification engine uses OpenMetadata context: anomaly type + downstream entity count + raw metrics to determine Critical/High/Medium/Low severity, which drives the routing decision (phone call vs Slack-only).

All 5 tools are tested against the live OpenMetadata sandbox (sandbox.open-metadata.org) with real data and are verified with dim_customers (12 columns, owner nick.acosta, 4 lineage nodes, 2 downstream entities: customer_metrics and executive_sales_summary).

Project description:
Command-line tool for OpenMetadata. Written in Rust.

Dynamic command surface generated from OpenMetadata's OpenAPI spec, plus hand-tuned "smart" commands for the common workflows (search, describe, lineage, quality, CSV import/export). Structured JSON output for scripts and agents. Ships an MCP server mode (omd mcp) so AI agents can drive OpenMetadata directly.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
omd is a client *for* OpenMetadata, not a project that consumes it as
> a dependency. Concretely:
>
> - Talks to OpenMetadata's REST API (`/api/v1/*`) over HTTPS via reqwest
>   with rustls. JWT bot tokens by default; `omd auth login --sso` does
>   OIDC PKCE through the browser for Google / Okta / Azure AD / Auth0.
> - Auto-generates the dynamic command surface from OpenMetadata's OpenAPI
>   spec (`/swagger.json` from the configured host) — 1,415 operations
>   across 82 tag groups become subcommands at runtime. Spec is cached
>   at `~/.omd/spec.json`, refreshable via `omd sync`, with a vendored
>   fallback for air-gapped setups.
> - Hand-written smart commands wrap the most-used flows: `search`
>   (Elasticsearch query API), `describe`, `lineage` (renders OpenMetadata's
>   lineage graph as tree / Mermaid / DOT / JSON), `edit` and `tag`
>   (JSON-patch against the entity), `quality` (test cases + results),
>   `import`/`export` (async CSV jobs with progress polling).
> - Includes JSON-patch routing for nested entities — e.g. column-level
>   tagging walks the FQN, fetches the parent table, and patches
>   `/columns/<idx>/tags` since OpenMetadata models columns inside their
>   parent table.
> - `omd mcp` runs a Model Context Protocol stdio server exposing 15
>   curated tools (`search`, `describe_entity`, `get_lineage`, `add_tag`,
>   `update_description`, `import_csv`, etc.) so AI agents in Claude
>   Desktop / Cursor / Claude Code can read and write the catalog
>   conversationally.
> - Tested against the 1.11.x server line via local docker-compose with
>   seeded sample data (databases, schemas, tables, columns, lineage
>   edges, classification tags).

Project description: FinGuard Sentinel is an Agentic AI-powered Data Risk Intelligence Dashboard. It bridges the gap between low-level metadata changes and high-level executive decision-making.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
In this project, we used OpenMetadata  as the central "nervous system" for data governance. It isn't just a static catalog; it is the engine that allows FinGuard Sentinel to map technical changes to business risks in real-time.

Here is a breakdown of how it’s integrated:
1. Automated Lineage Discovery (The "Blast Radius")

We use OpenMetadata’s Lineage API to programmatically discover relationships between financial tables.

    The Process: When a schema change is detected in a source table (like raw_transactions), the system queries OpenMetadata to find all downstream consumers.

    The Result: This allows us to calculate the "Blast Radius"—identifying exactly which fraud detection models, reconciliation ledgers, and compliance reports will be impacted by a single column change.

2. Event-Driven Governance via Webhooks

Instead of manual audits, we configured OpenMetadata Webhooks to send real-time JSON payloads to our FastAPI backend whenever an entityUpdated event occurs.

    The Impact: This transforms OpenMetadata from a documentation tool into an active security monitor. The moment a developer modifies a table schema, FinGuard receives the signal and begins its risk analysis.

3. Metadata Extraction & Search

We utilize the OpenMetadata Python SDK to perform deep searches across the data ecosystem.

    FQN Resolution: We use the search service to resolve simple table names into Fully Qualified Names (FQN).

    UUID Mapping: We retrieve unique entity IDs to ensure our risk engine is tracking the exact version of the data asset, preventing "false positives" from similarly named tables in different environments.

4. Unified Source of Truth

By leveraging the Standardized Metadata Schema, we ensure that our AI agent (Llama-3.1) receives high-quality, structured context.

    Contextual Feeding: We extract descriptions and tags from OpenMetadata and feed them into the AI prompt. This allows the AI to understand that a table isn't just "Table_A," but specifically the "Statutory Audit Ledger for Central Africa Operations," leading to much more accurate risk assessments.
How was your hackathon experience?: Spent a good chunk of time fighting strict Pydantic models, which taught us that sometimes the most robust solution is the one that handles "noisy" real-world data with the most grace. It was a good experience and we learnt so much!

Project description:
MetaFlux is an AI-driven Data Command Center designed to transform how organizations interact with their data catalogs. By integrating OpenMetadata with state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs), MetaFlux turns static metadata into a conversational, actionable intelligence hub.

Most data catalogs suffer from being passive repositories that are difficult to navigate for non-technical users. MetaFlux solves this by providing:

AI Data Navigator: A conversational chat interface that understands natural language queries about schemas, ownership, and data quality.
Automated Health Scoring: A proprietary A-F grading system that instantly communicates the reliability of any data asset.
Active Lineage & Impact Analysis: Interactive visualizations that not only show where data comes from but also predict the downstream "blast radius" of potential changes.
Governance Sentinel: Real-time PII detection and ownership tracking to ensure data stays secure and compliant.
MetaFlux isn't just a tool for seeing your metadata; it's a tool for talking to your data ecosystem.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
MetaFlux leverages OpenMetadata as the central nervous system for data observability and discovery. Instead of just a passive catalog, I transformed OpenMetadata's rich metadata into an active, AI-driven "Data Command Center."

Technical Implementation:
Unified Search & Discovery: I utilized the /search/query endpoint to build a "Google-like" experience for data assets, allowing users to find tables and dashboards across multiple sources (MySQL, Athena, etc.) using natural language.
Deep Lineage Integration: By consuming the /lineage API, MetaFlux provides both an interactive 2D visualization for "hopping" through data flows and an AI-driven Impact Analysis tool that predicts downstream consequences of schema changes.
Automated Data Health Scoring: I built a proprietary scoring engine that pulls metadata from /tables and /testCases. It calculates an A-F Health Grade based on four pillars:
Completeness: Description and tag coverage.
Reliability: Pass/fail status of data quality tests.
Governance: Ownership assignment.
Freshness: Usage and update frequency.
Security & PII Sentinel: I implemented a scanning layer that identifies PII (Personally Identifiable Information) tagged in OpenMetadata and proactively alerts users during chat interactions, ensuring compliance-first data access.
Entity Linking: Every conversation is grounded in the OpenMetadata entity model using entityLink formats, ensuring that the AI has a precise reference to the exact asset being discussed.
How was your hackathon experience?:
My experience while building MetaFlux was incredibly rewarding, primarily due to the extensibility of the OpenMetadata API. Working with the OpenMetadata sandbox was seamless. The comprehensive documentation helped me to focus on building premium UI/UX and AI logic rather than fighting with connectivity.

The biggest highlight was realizing how easily I could bridge the gap between static metadata and actionable insights. Within hours, I was able to turn a JSON response from a lineage API into a predictive impact radar that would take weeks to build from scratch.

One of the most interesting challenges was handling "name-to-FQN" resolution. I had to build a robust fallback layer that uses search to resolve human-friendly names into the strict Fully Qualified Names required by the metadata APIs—a perfect example of the last mile problem in AI tools.

This hackathon showed me that the future of data management isn't just about cataloging; it's about context. OpenMetadata provides the context, and MetaFlux provides the conversation.
I am walking away with a deep appreciation for the OpenMetadata community and a functional, premium feel application that I believe solves a real pain point for data teams globally.

Project description:
The Problem Modern data ecosystems are inherently fragmented. Data engineers, product managers, and software developers operate in heavily siloed environments. Data quality issues live in one platform, sprint planning in Jira, pipeline errors in Sentry, and codebase changes in GitHub. When a critical pipeline breaks or a data contract is breached, teams waste countless hours cross-referencing these disconnected tools to hunt down the root cause. This fragmentation leads to delayed incident resolution, misaligned product sprints, undetected governance violations, and severe developer burnout.

What Meridian Does Meridian is a centralized, AI-driven Intelligence Hub designed to eliminate this fragmentation. It acts as an active, automated operational brain that ingests, correlates, and analyzes real-time signals across your entire engineering and data stack. Powered by an event-driven backend and a centralized Llama-3-70B reasoning engine, Meridian doesn't just display passive metrics—it autonomously predicts sprint delays, flags team burnout risks, and instantly correlates schema-breaking code changes with downstream data failures.

The Central Pillar: OpenMetadata At the very core of Meridian sits OpenMetadata. Rather than building a redundant data catalog, Meridian leverages OpenMetadata as its foundational source of truth for the entire data estate, transforming it from a passive catalog into a proactive command center. By deeply integrating OpenMetadata's rich APIs, Meridian allows users to natively search tables, inspect schemas, and trace end-to-end data lineage without ever leaving the dashboard. More importantly, Meridian utilizes OpenMetadata's lineage graph to automatically calculate the downstream "blast radius" of code changes, and relies on its classification system to actively enforce data governance (such as PII masking policies) in real-time.

The Integration Ecosystem To provide infinite observability depth, Meridian seamlessly correlates signals across a full suite of essential engineering tools:

OpenMetadata: Acts as the central nervous system, providing live table schemas, data quality test results, and deep lineage graphs to trace upstream/downstream impact.
GitHub: Monitors Pull Requests, commit velocities, and after-hours activity. When a PR alters a database schema, Meridian instantly catches it and uses OpenMetadata's lineage to warn the team of potential downstream BI/reporting breakages.
Jira: Tracks sprint health, scope creep, and blocked issues. Meridian's AI correlates delayed sprints with active data pipeline outages, allowing stakeholders to see exactly why a project is off track.
Sentry: Ingests application and data pipeline error logs. Meridian's AI agents correlate these error spikes directly with recent GitHub deployments or OpenMetadata schema modifications.
Slack: Serves as the real-time alerting layer. Whether it's a PII violation tagged in OpenMetadata or a schema-breaking PR in GitHub, the Meridian Slack Bot instantly routes contextual "Governance" and "Schema Impact" alerts to the relevant engineering channels.
dbt Cloud & PagerDuty: Monitors transformation job success rates and automatically escalates critical, unresolved data incidents to on-call data engineers via PagerDuty.
Why It Is Necessary Meridian is necessary because modern data infrastructure has become too complex to monitor manually. By unifying deep data governance (OpenMetadata) with daily engineering operations (GitHub/Jira/Sentry) under the umbrella of an autonomous AI reasoning engine, Meridian provides teams with unparalleled cross-domain context. It ensures data contracts are respected, accelerates incident resolution, protects team health, and ultimately turns fragmented tooling into a single, cohesive, highly data-focused workflow.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
OpenMetadata serves as the foundational data intelligence layer within Meridian's architecture. Rather than building a redundant catalog, we deeply integrated OpenMetadata as our primary source of truth for all data assets, schema states, and data lineage.

Specifically, we utilized OpenMetadata to:
- Map Blast Radius: When our webhooks detect a schema-breaking Pull Request in GitHub, Meridian queries OpenMetadata's lineage graph to instantly identify exactly which downstream tables, fact tables, and executive data marts will be impacted.
- Enforce Governance: We utilize OpenMetadata's classification system to track PII. If an event occurs on a flagged table, Meridian triggers a real-time Governance Alert in our Slack workspace.
- Unified Discovery: We proxied OpenMetadata's search and entity APIs directly into our Next.js frontend. This allows users to search their data estate, view table schemas, and trace end-to-end lineage graphs without ever having to context-switch out of the Meridian dashboard.
How was your hackathon experience?: The hackathon experience was incredibly rewarding and fast-paced! Project description:
The idea is simple.

Tools can detect problems in data, but fixing them still takes time. Someone has to understand the issue, write a fix, test it, and then apply it.

AegisDB does that part.

When a test fails, it checks what went wrong, looks at past fixes, tries a solution in a safe test setup, and then shows it to the user. You can approve it from the UI or Slack.

After applying the fix, it also updates everything. Logs, notes, and details are saved automatically so no one has to remember what happened later.

So instead of just finding problems, it actually helps fix them.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
OpenMetadata is the base of this project.

It runs data tests and tells AegisDB when something fails. AegisDB also pulls extra details like table info and column types to better understand the issue.

After fixing the problem, AegisDB updates OpenMetadata again. It adds notes about what happened and marks the table as fixed.

So it’s not just reading from it, it’s also writing back to it.

This way, anyone checking later can see what went wrong and how it was fixed.

Project description:
It's 3 a.m. Your pipeline broke. OpenMetadata shows fifteen upstream things that changed today. One is the cause. Fourteen are coincidences. The catalog can't tell them apart — and "the most recent change wins" is wrong half the time.

CausalOps fixes the half. We treat OpenMetadata's lineage as a causal graph, fit a structural causal model on your change events and DQ test results, and answer the two questions catalogs can't:

Why did this fail? — backdoor adjustment over the DAG with propensity-score matching. The schema change three hours ago, with effect 0.92 and 95% CI [0.71, 1.00], not the owner rotation that just happened.

What breaks if I deploy this? — Monte-Carlo intervention through the lineage subgraph. discount_code → campaign_attribution at 83% probability. Patch the join first.

Every answer ships with confidence intervals, placebo p-values, and subset stability — receipts for the claim, not vibes. Validated: 80% top-1 vs 50% recency baseline. Same engine in the web UI and over MCP, so OpenMetadata's chat (or Claude Desktop) can call it inline.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
OpenMetadata is the source of truth for everything CausalOps reasons over. We don't fork it, we don't shadow it — we use it as a graph substrate.

Ingest. A scheduled BullMQ worker (pollLineage, pollEvents, pollTestResults) calls OM's REST API every 1–10 minutes — GET /lineage/table/name/{fqn} for the DAG, GET /events for change history, GET /dataQuality/testCases/testCaseResults for DQ outcomes — and projects the data into TimescaleDB hypertables for fast 30-day windows.

Reason. Lineage edges become a NetworkX DiGraph in our Python worker. ChangeEvents are encoded as binary treatments, DQ failures as outcomes. Backdoor adjustment over the DAG identifies the minimal covariate set; propensity-score matching estimates the do-effect. The whole engine inherits OM's notion of identity (FQNs), authorship, and column-level lineage when present.

Write back. After every high-confidence RCA we PATCH the entity's extension field — causalOpsRiskScore, causalOpsTopCause, causalOpsLastAnalysis — so the OM UI shows our verdict alongside its native metadata. We also register an event subscription so live ChangeEvents flow into our system in near-real-time.

Expose. An MCP server wraps the four tools so OM's chat panel and Claude Desktop can call them directly without leaving the catalog.
How was your hackathon experience?: Shipped: counterfactual RCA, intervention simulator, an MCP server for OpenMetadata's chat, a back-test harness validating 80% top-1 vs 50% baseline on 20 ground-truth incidents. Didn't ship: column-level DoWhy with SQL-transformation-aware propagation, time-varying confounders via Granger / synthetic control, Slack narration. The MVP was always going to be the engine plus the receipts (CI + placebo + stability) — everything else is on the roadmap. The hackathon scope was the right scope to prove the idea.

Project description:
LineageGuard : A Semantic Blast Radius for OpenMetadata

LineageGuard answers one question every analytics engineer faces: "If I make this schema change, what will actually break, and who will feel it?"

It walks OpenMetadata's lineage graph downstream from a given table, fetches governance signals (tier, owner, glossary terms, data contracts) for each affected entity, and classifies them into CRITICAL, HIGH, WARNING, or INFO using a deterministic 4-level ranking algorithm — no AI reasoning involved.

Exposed as both a CLI (CI-ready with non-zero exit codes on CRITICAL findings) and a Model Context Protocol server, LineageGuard lets Claude Desktop and other AI assistants answer "what breaks if I drop this column?" with graph-grounded analysis that cites real glossary terms, real owners, and real tiers.

The architectural thesis: metadata as deterministic code, not documentation. The engine is pure Python; the LLM only narrates structured findings.
Deployed link to project: LineageGuard is a developer-side tool — it runs locally as a CLI and MCP server against a local OpenMetadata instance. See the README "Quick Start" for reproducible setup: clone, docker compose up, pip install, python seed.py, run.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
LineageGuard uses OpenMetadata as its source of truth for metadata, lineage, and governance throughout.

Ingestion: A custom seed.py script creates the demo metadata graph via OpenMetadata's REST API — services, tables, dashboards, a glossary with business terms, team ownership, and 5 lineage edges. The script is idempotent and reproducible.

API consumption: An OpenMetadataClient authenticates via Personal Access Token and consumes:
- GET /tables/name/{fqn} for entity resolution
- GET /lineage/{entityType}/{id} for downstream lineage traversal
- GET /glossaryTerms/name/{fqn} for glossary enrichment
- GET /teams/name/{name} for owner/domain resolution

Semantic layer usage: The ranker reads four OpenMetadata governance primitives — Tier classifications, ownership references, glossary term attachments, and Data Contract signals (with a Classification-tag fallback when the Data Contract API is unavailable). Each is weighted deterministically to produce severity.

MCP integration: LineageGuard ships as an MCP server that exposes analyze_semantic_impact and get_entity_governance as tools to AI assistants. This implements OpenMetadata's vision of metadata as deterministic code for AI agents — the engine produces structured findings, and LLMs like Claude only narrate them.

Read-only by design. LineageGuard never mutates OpenMetadata state. The seed script is a separate demo-preparation tool, not part of the analysis pipeline.
Link to pull requests that you made to t: N/A — Project Track submission. Did not submit to the PR Track.
How was your hackathon experience?: Strong learning curve. I came in with Python basics and limited backend experience. The hackathon pushed me to deeply understand semantic metadata, lineage graphs, and the Model Context Protocol. The hardest discipline was resisting the temptation to let an LLM "decide" severity — holding the line on a deterministic engine is what made the project actually correct. OpenMetadata's API is thoughtfully designed, and MCP's stdio transport is cleaner than expected once the protocol quirks are understood. I'd do it again.

Project description:
Data pipeline failures cost data teams countless hours of manual investigation. When a dashboard breaks or a data quality test fails, engineers must manually trace upstream dependencies to find the root cause and downstream dependencies to assess the impact. Data Doctor solves this by acting as an intelligent, automated diagnostic system built entirely on top of OpenMetadata.

Data Doctor is a standalone Command Center (built with a Python FastAPI backend and a sleek React 19 frontend) that drastically reduces mean time to resolution (MTTR). Given a failing target entity, it connects to OpenMetadata's APIs and executes a deterministic analysis in under 3 seconds:

Bidirectional Lineage Traversal: It executes a Breadth-First Search (BFS) upstream to hunt for the root cause and downstream to map the incident's "blast radius" (affected dashboards, models, and tables).
Production-Grade Anomaly Detection: As it traverses the graph, it runs 6 distinct detectors evaluating OpenMetadata profiles, test results, and execution statuses. It detects Pipeline Failures (crashed Airflow DAGs), Schema Drift, Data Quality Failures, Stale Data, Volume Anomalies, and Distribution Drift—all without issuing a single SELECT query against the data warehouse.
Transparent Confidence Scoring: Instead of relying on an AI "black box" to guess what went wrong, Data Doctor uses a transparent mathematical formula to score the probability of a root cause based on signal strength, topological distance, and noise penalties.
Automated Governance: High-severity incidents trigger programmatic tagging via the OpenMetadata API, instantly stamping affected assets with DataQuality.Critical or Status.Unreliable to warn downstream consumers.
Hybrid AI Remediation Engine: We integrated Groq's fast LLMs purely as a formatting layer. Once the deterministic engine identifies the fix, the AI drafts safe, executable SQL rollback scripts, formats Slack alerts, and generates professional Markdown incident reports.
Data Doctor demonstrates the true power of a central metadata repository. By deeply integrating with OpenMetadata’s Lineage, Profiler, Test Cases, and Search APIs, it turns a passive catalog into an active, self-diagnosing data observability platform.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
Data Doctor uses OpenMetadata not just as a catalog, but as a live, queryable fact store to power a deterministic diagnostic engine, completely avoiding the need to issue SELECT queries against production data warehouses. At its core, we utilize the Lineage API to perform bidirectional Breadth-First Search (BFS) traversals—navigating upstream to pinpoint root causes and downstream to map the incident's blast radius.

To detect anomalies, we read pre-computed statistical summaries via the Table Profile API (flagging volume and schema drift), and query the Test Case API to catch failed data quality contracts. Because OpenMetadata treats pipelines as first-class lineage nodes, we also read executionStatus metadata to attribute data failures directly to crashed orchestrator DAGs. We track lastUpdated timestamps to catch stale data against SLAs, and utilize the Entity Versioning API to parse changeDescription payloads for tracking historical schema mutations. Finally, when an incident is detected, Data Doctor acts via the PATCH Entity API to automatically apply "DataQuality.Critical" tags across the entire affected blast radius, ensuring downstream consumers are warned directly in the OpenMetadata UI.

Please refer to docs/openmetadata-usage.docx in our GitHub repository for a complete breakdown of OpenMetadata usage.
How was your hackathon experience?:
My hackathon experience was incredibly rewarding. Coming in, I was entirely new to OpenMetadata, but attending the "Kickoff Livestream: Getting Started with OpenMetadata" really set the stage for me. It provided a clear, practical roadmap that made diving into the ecosystem feel approachable rather than overwhelming. As I started building Data Doctor, I found myself genuinely fascinated by how beautifully engineered the platform is. The API-first architecture, the way pipelines are treated as first-class lineage nodes, and the sheer depth of the profiling and metadata capabilities are fantastic.

Because I was so intrigued by the platform's potential, I spent a significant portion of the hackathon deeply researching industry standards in data observability and data governance to ensure I was building something that adhered to real-world best practices. This rigorous exploration heavily influenced how I designed the root cause traversal and blast radius mapping features, which is reflected in detail in the research.docx, specs.docx, and decision.docx files included in my GitHub repository. Overall, it was an amazing learning experience that completely changed how I think about modern metadata management.

Project description:
MetaTree brings OpenMetadata to the exact places where data decisions are made: pull requests, terminals, VS Code, and AI tools.

Every broken dashboard, failed pipeline, and confusing downstream incident usually starts the same way: a small SQL, dbt, or schema change that looked safe at the time. OpenMetadata already knows the context needed to prevent this: lineage, ownership, quality, tags, descriptions, and governance metadata. But that context often lives outside the developer workflow.

MetaTree shifts OpenMetadata left.

It turns OpenMetadata from a passive catalog into an active developer guardrail. Our GitHub Action analyzes every PR, resolves changed assets against OpenMetadata, walks downstream lineage, and comments directly on the pull request with the dashboards, pipelines, and tables that could be impacted. Our Rust CLI, ometa, gives developers fast terminal access to search, lineage, asset details, data quality, metadata patching, and MCP-powered AI workflows. Our VS Code extension brings OpenMetadata into the editor with hover cards, ownership context, quality status, tags, columns, and lineage exploration while developers write SQL and dbt.

MetaTree answers the question every data team should ask before merge:

What will break if we ship this?

Built deeply on OpenMetadata’s REST APIs, lineage, search, data quality, governance metadata, JWT authentication, and MCP ecosystem, MetaTree makes metadata unavoidable in the best way. Developers keep their flow. Reviewers get instant blast-radius analysis. Governance becomes part of daily engineering work. Teams prevent data breakages before they reach production.

MetaTree is OpenMetadata where developers work.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
MetaTree is built directly on top of OpenMetadata and uses it as the central source of truth for developer workflows.

We use OpenMetadata’s search APIs to resolve changed SQL, dbt, and schema entities from pull requests into real catalog assets. Once an asset is identified, MetaTree uses OpenMetadata entity metadata to fetch owners, tags, descriptions, columns, and governance context. We use OpenMetadata lineage APIs to walk downstream dependencies and generate PR impact reports showing which tables, dashboards, and pipelines may be affected by a change.

MetaTree also uses OpenMetadata’s data quality APIs to surface test status and failing checks inside the CLI and VS Code extension. For AI workflows, our CLI includes an MCP proxy that connects MCP-aware tools to OpenMetadata while handling JWT authentication.

In short, MetaTree turns OpenMetadata’s discovery, lineage, governance, observability, REST APIs, and MCP capabilities into a developer-first workflow across GitHub Actions, terminal, and VS Code.
How was your hackathon experience?:
Our hackathon experience was genuinely exciting and highly educational. We loved exploring OpenMetadata as an open-source project and understanding how much it can do across discovery, lineage, governance, observability, and developer workflows.

During the hackathon, we experimented with multiple ideas and approaches before converging on MetaTree. That exploration helped us understand the OpenMetadata ecosystem more deeply and think about where metadata can create the most impact in real engineering workflows. We especially enjoyed building with OpenMetadata’s APIs and seeing how metadata can move beyond a catalog UI into CI/CD, terminals, editors, and AI tools.

Overall, the hackathon pushed us to learn fast, build practically, and think creatively about the future of metadata-driven development. It was a great experience working with open source and building something we would actually want to use ourselves.

Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
MetaSift sits on top of OpenMetadata as an AI-powered metadata analyst layer. It integrates through three complementary channels:

REST API (/api/v1) — bulk reads + gated writes

Paginated /v1/tables fetches to hydrate a local DuckDB cache
Per-table /v1/lineage/... walks to build an om_lineage table
/v1/dataQuality/testCases ingestion for the DQ track
PATCH with JSON-patch for description and column-tag write-backs
PUT /v1/teams + ownership patches in the seed script
MCP server (/mcp) — read-only agent-facing discovery

Loaded via ai_sdk.AISdk(...).mcp.as_langchain_tools()
Allowlisted to search_metadata, get_entity_details, get_entity_lineage
Write-capable ops (e.g. patch_entity) are deliberately excluded so the review queue stays the only write surface
openmetadata-ingestion SDK — pinned at server version 1.9.4 in pyproject.toml for pydantic/schema compatibility on write-backs

On top of these channels, MetaSift addresses six "Back to the Metadata" hackathon issues (#26608, #26659, #26660, #26658, #26661, #25146) — covering conversational catalog chat, plain-English DQ failure explanations, AI-powered DQ test recommendations, DQ impact scoring via lineage, automated fix proposals, and a PII lineage governance layer. Project description:
We started from a small scaffold so the repo had a clear shape early. Then we spent real time on the boring but important part: understanding OpenMetadata MCP tools, params, and return shapes, and writing that down so we did not guess in code.

After that we brought up OpenMetadata locally with docker compose helpers and a seed dataset so search and demos had real tables to hit. The next big step was the MCP client plus a LangGraph skeleton so the model could call tools in a controlled way, not ad hoc scripts.

From there the work split into vertical slices. We added typed wrappers around the main MCP tools, wired a React chat UI to the FastAPI chat route, and tightened CI so lint, types, security gates, and tests stayed honest as the repo grew.

Phase two style work showed up as governance ideas in code: a session store for human in the loop confirm and cancel, a small FSM for governance state, auto classification that stops at a proposal until a human says yes, and an NL query path that routes intents in a more deterministic way than pure model vibes.

We added drift polling so the catalog does not silently drift away from what we think we tagged. Lineage impact work tried to summarize blast radius before writes. Multi MCP meant wiring GitHub MCP next to OpenMetadata MCP so one conversation could touch catalog metadata and a repo style action in demo scope.

Near the end we chased integration coverage, demo and seed scripts, and Playwright flows so a judge or teammate could repeat the story without hand holding. The last commits were mostly docs and diagrams so someone new can read the repo once and understand the trust boundaries.
Deployed link to project: We did not ship a public URL for version one on purpose. The backend binds to loopback and the threat model treats this as a laptop style demo. If the form allows honesty, say not publicly deployed and point to the GitHub Actions CI badge and the README run steps. If you must paste a link, use a short unlisted screen recording host only after you upload a walkthrough, not a live internet exposed API.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
OpenMetadata is the system of record for metadata in our demo. We do not fork OpenMetadata. We talk to it as a client using the official data ai sdk path to MCP over HTTP, with a bot style token for auth in local setups.

We use MCP tools the way OpenMetadata intends: search entities, read details, work with lineage context, and propose or perform catalog updates depending on the tool and our gates. The agent is only a orchestration layer. Permissions and visibility still come from what that OpenMetadata user or bot can do.

We also used OpenMetadata as a realistic target for governance workflows: seed data with many tables, reindex search when needed, and drift checks that compare what we stored as intended tags against what the catalog shows later.
How was your hackathon experience?:
It felt like building a thin product on top of a real platform constraint set. Early days were mostly reading, seeding, and proving one round trip from agent to OpenMetadata. Middle days were the messier merge weeks where UI, sessions, and governance crossed paths and we had to resolve conflicts without breaking the layer rules we wrote for ourselves.

The part that stuck with me is how fast “demo pretty” tries to fight “safe by default”. We kept pushing writes behind confirm, kept tests next to features, and accepted that some production ideas like public deploy and per user OAuth are honestly out of scope for version one.

Team wise it was a mix of deep solo focus and PRs that needed a second pair of eyes on CI. Stressful in the last stretch, but the repo history reads like a real engineering arc, not a single giant dump on the last day.

The agent is only a orchestration layer. Permissions and visibility still come from what that OpenMetadata user or bot can do.

Project description:
Metadata Change Guard - 
An automated CI/CD policy engine designed to intercept data schema changes before they are deployed to prevent silent downstream breakages. By acting as a pre-deploy gatekeeper, the engine simulates proposed changes such as dropping a column or modifying a data type against live OpenMetadata context. 
It recursively traverses the metadata lineage graph to map the exact blast radius, and evaluates a multi-factor risk matrix based on business criticality, data governance tags, and current data quality metrics. Instead of relying on tribal knowledge or failing silently in production, the engine deterministically decides whether to allow, guard, or block the release, giving data teams immediate visibility and actionable remediation steps.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata: Used OpenMetadata as the foundational source of truth for my automated CI/CD policy engine. Whenever a schema change is proposed, the engine queries OpenMetadata's REST API to dynamically extract the impacted entity's context including governance tags (like PII), owners, data quality SLA status, and business criticality tiers. It then pulls the entity's lineage DAG and performs a recursive graph traversal to map the exact downstream blast radius. The engine feeds all this context into a multi-factor risk scoring matrix that automatically decides whether to allow, guard, or block a risky deployment.

Project description: LineageGuard:  real-time risk intelligence layer for data pipelines, detects schema changes via OpenMetadata, traces the downstream blast radius, and delivers an AI-generated financial impact assessment instantly.

I pointed these webhooks at LineageGuard's /webhook endpoint so the system reacts instantly to any change.                                                          
                                                                                                                                          
  4. API for Entity Resolution                                                                                                            
                                                                                                                                          
When a webhook arrives with just a table name, I call the OpenMetadata API to:                                                          
                                                                                                                                          
  - Search for the table by name → get the Fully Qualified Name (FQN)                                                                     
  - Resolve the FQN to a UUID                                                                                                             
  - Fetch the full lineage graph for that entity                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                          
  This logic lives in services/openmetadata.py.

Project description:
MetaReview is an AI-powered PR guardrail for data teams that reviews SQL changes before they are merged. It analyzes pull request diffs, enriches them using OpenMetadata, and highlights risks like sensitive fields, deprecated columns, and downstream impact.

Without executing queries or accessing data, it generates clear, actionable reviews directly in GitHub, helping teams catch issues early and ship safer data changes.
Describe how you have used OpenMetadata:
OpenMetadata is used as the core metadata layer in MetaReview. When a pull request contains SQL changes, the system extracts the referenced tables, columns, and dbt references, and queries OpenMetadata APIs to fetch context such as tags, PII indicators, deprecated fields, and downstream lineage.
This metadata is then used to assess the risk of the change: higher risk is assigned when sensitive data, deprecated columns, or widely used downstream assets are involved. Based on this, MetaReview generates a structured review comment with a risk summary and recommendations, which is posted directly on the GitHub pull request.
Importantly, OpenMetadata is a real runtime dependency in the system. MetaReview does not execute SQL or access warehouse data; it relies entirely on OpenMetadata to provide context for safe and informed PR reviews.
